Import direction is out of scope for this rule, so that mismatch does not affect the verdict.

RandomIdGenerator is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the application port IdGenerator by delegating to node:crypto's randomUUID. Wrapping a system or platform capability behind a port is a normal infrastructure job. The file holds no business rules, domain invariants, application orchestration or presentation logic. Import direction is out of scope.

SystemClock is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the application-layer Clock port by wrapping the system clock (new Date()). Reaching the system/runtime is an infrastructure job. The file contains no business rules, no orchestration and no presentation logic, so its only responsibility fits its declared infrastructure layer.

The module is one cohesive application layer for ordering and stock: use cases, the errors they share, interfaces for time and ids (Clock, IdGenerator), DTOs with their mapping functions, and one error classifier. Use cases that need an existing order or its products get them through EntityLookupService. RegisterProductUseCase calls products.findById directly, but only to reject a duplicate id with ConflictError, which the lookup service does not offer, so it does not bypass it. Each failure kind has one class in ApplicationErrors.ts, and only ErrorClassification.ts maps them to categories. Each mapping function sits next to its DTO. Two use cases both check a status string with the domain's isOrderStatus and throw ValidationError, which is ordinary input validation. Three use cases repeat a loop that saves each changed product. Neither counts as a duplicated invariant or a split concern.

The src/domain module covers one concern: order fulfilment and stock allocation. Its files use the module's abstractions consistently. One error hierarchy (DomainError) is used everywhere. The order lifecycle rules live only in OrderStatus.ts and Order uses them. Merging lines for the same product lives only in OrderLine.consolidate. StockAllocationService changes stock only through Product's public methods and never alters Product state directly. The repository interfaces are defined over the module's own aggregates. One small duplication exists: the positive-integer quantity check appears in both OrderLine.of and Product's assertPositiveInteger. It is a minor input guard, not a business invariant split across files, so it does not make the module fail.

The infrastructure module serves one concern: adapting the application layer to the outside world. It has three kinds of file: adapters (in-memory repositories, SystemClock, RandomIdGenerator, HTTP controllers), wiring (CatalogueModule, OrderModule, Persistence, HttpApp) and the composition root (server.ts). The module's own building blocks are used consistently. Both controllers parse request bodies only through RequestParsing. Both feature modules get their stores only from the shared Persistence object. Mapping errors to HTTP status codes happens only in ErrorMiddleware via classifyError. Neither the parsing checks nor the error-to-status mapping is duplicated anywhere else in the module, and no file goes around these shared pieces.

src/application/AdvanceOrderUseCase.ts does the work an application-layer use case is supposed to do. It checks the incoming status string, loads the order and its products through a lookup service, and leaves the state transition to the domain (order.advanceTo). It leaves the stock arithmetic to a domain service (StockAllocationService.dispatch), saves through domain repository interfaces, and maps the result to a DTO. The file holds no persistence code, transport code or framework code. It also holds no business calculations of its own. The one borderline spot is the check `if (order.status === 'shipped')`. It decides when stock is dispatched. This is coordination between two aggregates (the order and the products), not a business calculation, and the rule itself is carried out by the domain service. Coordinating effects across aggregates after a state change is a normal job for a use case.

CancelOrderUseCase.execute does only application-layer orchestration. It loads entities through the injected EntityLookupService. It hands the cancellation rule to the domain entity (order.cancel) and stock release to the domain StockAllocationService. It saves through the repository interfaces declared in the domain layer, gets the time from an injected Clock port, and maps the result to an application DTO. The file holds no business rules of its own: it makes no state checks, does no stock arithmetic and has no conditional logic. It also has no persistence code, transport handling or framework annotations. Creating StockAllocationService directly is a wiring choice, not a responsibility from another layer.

EntityLookupService is an application-layer helper that orchestrates loading aggregates through domain repository abstractions and throws an application-level NotFoundError when an aggregate is missing. Use-case orchestration and application error signaling belong in the application layer. The file has no persistence implementation (no SQL, ORM, or storage access), no transport or framework logic, and no domain business invariants. It only checks for existence and builds a map. No ADR prose was given.

GetOrderUseCase is a thin application-layer use case. Its one method, execute, uses an injected application service (EntityLookupService.requireOrder) to fetch an order and maps the result to an OrderDto. Coordinating a lookup and mapping to a DTO is what the application layer is for. The file has no persistence code, no transport or framework logic, and no business rules that should live in the domain layer.

The file only declares a port interface, IdGenerator, with a single method, nextId(): string. An application-layer port that a use case consumes and infrastructure implements is a normal application responsibility. The file contains no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic. The graph agrees: PlaceOrderUseCase injects it through its constructor and RandomIdGenerator in infrastructure implements it.

PlaceOrderUseCase does only what an application layer should do: it orchestrates the use case. It turns the incoming command into domain objects using the domain's own factories (OrderLine.of, Order.place). It hands stock reservation to a domain service (StockAllocationService.reserve). It saves the results through repository interfaces defined in the domain (OrderRepository, ProductRepository). It gets ids and the current time through application interfaces (IdGenerator, Clock), and it converts the result into a DTO. The file contains no business rules of its own: the order-placement rules stay in Order.place and the reservation rules stay in StockAllocationService. It also contains no persistence, transport or framework code, since there is no SQL, HTTP, ORM or decorators. Creating the domain service directly with `new` is a wiring choice, not a responsibility that belongs to another layer.

The file sits in the application layer. It defines application-boundary data shapes: an output DTO (ProductStockDto) and an input command (RegisterProductCommand). It also has a simple mapping function (toProductStockDto) that copies fields from the domain Product into the DTO. Use cases need DTOs, commands and domain-to-DTO mapping, so all of these belong in the application layer. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or HTTP logic. It also has no business rules: 'available' is read from the domain entity, not calculated here. So nothing in the file belongs to another layer.

src/domain/DomainErrors.ts only defines domain error types for business-rule violations: an abstract DomainError base class and three subclasses (InvalidValueError, InsufficientStockError, InvalidTransitionError). Each one holds domain data such as productId, requested and available quantities, or orderId and the from/to statuses, and builds a domain-level message. The file has no persistence, transport (for example HTTP status codes), framework or presentation logic. It also doesn't map errors to outside representations, which seems to be done in src/application/ErrorClassification.ts. Every responsibility here fits the domain layer.

src/domain/OrderLine.ts is a pure domain value object. Its static factory 'of' enforces invariants: the product id must not be empty and the quantity must be a positive integer. A violation throws the domain error InvalidValueError. The static 'consolidate' method holds a domain rule that merges lines for the same product so each product appears once. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, presentation or use-case orchestration logic. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/OrderRepository.ts only declares a repository port: an interface written in domain terms (Order, OrderStatus). It has no persistence implementation, transport or framework code. The concrete storage lives in src/infrastructure/InMemoryOrderRepository.ts, which implements this interface. Putting a repository interface in the domain layer is a normal domain responsibility in layered and hexagonal designs, so nothing here belongs to a different layer kind.

src/domain/OrderStatus.ts sits in the domain layer, and everything in it is a domain concern. It defines the order status value set and a type guard. It also holds the business rules for the fulfilment sequence and for which statuses can still be cancelled. There is no persistence, transport, framework, I/O or orchestration logic in the file, so it fits the domain role.

src/domain/Product.ts is a pure domain entity. It holds the product's identity and stock state and enforces stock rules. The create factory validates input. The reserve, release and dispatch methods follow the stock rules. The assertPositiveInteger and assertNonNegativeInteger helpers check that values are valid integers. Errors are raised as domain errors. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, serialization or orchestration logic, so every responsibility fits the domain layer.

The file only declares the ProductRepository port interface, typed against the Product domain entity. A repository port is a standard domain-layer abstraction. It contains no persistence implementation, transport or framework code, and no application orchestration. The concrete implementation, InMemoryProductRepository, lives in the infrastructure layer and implements this interface. Application use cases receive the interface through constructor injection.

src/domain/StockAllocationService.ts is a pure domain service. It applies business rules to domain entities: all-or-nothing stock reservation across several products, plus release and dispatch. It contains no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic. It works on data that is passed in (OrderLine[] and a Map of Products) and raises domain errors. Loading and saving the products is left to the application use cases that call it. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/infrastructure/CatalogueModule.ts passes the rule. It is a composition root: it builds the application use cases from persistence adapters and hands them to a controller. Wiring dependencies together is the outer infrastructure layer's job. The file contains no business rules, validation, domain decisions or persistence logic of its own. It only creates and connects objects.

src/infrastructure/HttpApp.ts is the HTTP composition point. It builds an Express app, adds JSON body parsing, mounts the controller routers at '/orders' and '/products', and registers the not-found and error middleware. All of this is transport and framework wiring, which belongs in the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, domain calculations or application orchestration. No ADR prose was given.

OrderController.ts is an Express HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer. Each of its jobs fits that layer. It sets up routes, parses and checks the shape of request input with the RequestParsing helpers, maps the input to application commands, sends the work to application use cases, and writes JSON responses with HTTP status codes. Those are all transport concerns. It does not contain business rules: order state changes, cancellation rules and quantity limits are all handed off to the use cases. The parsing only checks types and structure (for example, that a field is a string, number or array). It does not check domain rules.

ProductController is an Express HTTP adapter, and that is an infrastructure responsibility. It sets up routes, parses and checks the request body using the RequestParsing helpers, hands the work to application use cases, and maps the results to HTTP status codes and JSON. It has no business rules (for example, no stock rules or product invariants) and no persistence logic. Checking the request shape (string or number fields) is transport-level parsing, not domain logic. Every responsibility fits the infrastructure layer.

src/infrastructure/RandomIdGenerator.ts is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the application-layer port IdGenerator by delegating to the platform's crypto API (node:crypto randomUUID). Wrapping a technical, platform-specific capability behind a port is the job of the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, domain decisions, orchestration or presentation logic. It has a single technical responsibility that fits its declared layer kind.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the composition root and process entry point. It reads the PORT environment variable, builds the in-memory persistence, wires the controllers together with their concrete adapters (RandomIdGenerator, SystemClock), creates the HTTP app and starts listening. Configuration, dependency wiring and transport startup all belong in the infrastructure layer. The file contains no business rules, validation or domain decisions, so every responsibility in it fits its declared layer.

The src/application module forms one coherent unit: the order-fulfilment application layer. Each file is either a use case with one `execute` method or a helper those use cases share (dtos.ts, OrderDtoMapper.ts, OrderLoader.ts). The shared abstractions are used consistently: - Every use case that returns an order uses `toOrderDto`. - Every use case that loads one order by id uses `loadOrder`, so the not-found check exists in exactly one place. - Stock side effects always go through `StockReservationService`. - Order state changes are left to domain methods (`Order.place`, `advanceTo`, `cancel`). ListOrdersUseCase calls `findByStatus`/`findAll` directly, which is correct: it loads a collection, not one order by id. ListStockLevelsUseCase builds `StockLevelDto` inline, but that mapping exists only there, so nothing is duplicated. ListStockLevelsUseCase is about stock rather than orders, but it belongs to the same fulfilment context and follows the same use-case/DTO pattern, so the module is not split into unrelated concerns. No rule is duplicated and no module abstraction is bypassed.

The src/domain module covers one concern: order fulfilment with stock reservation. Order status rules (the status list, the forward-only sequence, the cancellable set) live only in OrderStatus.ts, and Order.ts uses the nextStatus and isCancellable helpers instead of copying them. Quantity validation lives only in Quantity.of. Order and Product take Quantity objects rather than re-checking raw numbers. Stock rules (available, canReserve) live in Product. StockReservationService goes through ProductRepository and the Product methods, so it does not bypass the module's abstractions. Its up-front canReserve check makes a reservation all-or-nothing. That check calls Product.canReserve, so it is not a duplicated rule. All errors extend one DomainError base class. Clock, IdGenerator and the two repository interfaces are consistent ports, and both repositories document the same synchronous design. No unrelated concerns, duplicated invariants or bypassed abstractions were found.

Every file in the module is an infrastructure adapter. Each one implements a domain port or connects the app to the outside world. - **Persistence:** InMemoryOrderRepository and InMemoryProductRepository. - **System services:** SystemClock and UuidIdGenerator. - **HTTP:** OrderController, StockController, requestParsers and errorHandler. - **Composition and bootstrap:** app.ts, catalogueSeed.ts and server.ts. The files use the abstractions the same way throughout: - Both repositories store snapshots and rebuild entities through `restore()`. - The controllers only call use cases. - `catalogueSeed` saves products through the `ProductRepository` port and builds them with `Product.create`, so it does not bypass the domain factory. - `requestParsers` reuses the domain's `isOrderStatus` and `ValidationError` instead of keeping its own list of statuses. Its doc comment says business rules stay in the domain. Each rule lives in one place: - The mapping from errors to HTTP status exists only in errorHandler's `statusFor`. - The mapping from URL actions to target statuses (`ACTIONS`) exists only in OrderController. The repositories look alike, but each one is a different port, so that is not duplication.

AdvanceOrderUseCase.execute does normal application-layer orchestration. It loads the aggregate through a repository port, hands the state-transition rule to the domain (order.advanceTo(target, this.clock.now())), calls a domain service, saves through the port and maps the result to a DTO. It contains no persistence details, transport handling or framework code. The one branch, `if (target === 'shipped') this.stock.dispatch(order.lines)`, coordinates a side effect across a second collaborator after the domain transition has been checked. Coordinating collaborators like this is the use case's job. It does not compute or validate a business invariant. You could argue the shipped-means-dispatch link belongs in a domain event or in the domain service, but that is a design choice, not a clear layer violation. No ADR prose was given to say otherwise.

CancelOrderUseCase does what an application-layer use case should do. It loads the aggregate through a helper, hands the cancellation rule to the domain entity (order.cancel), releases stock through a domain service port, saves through a repository abstraction and returns a DTO. It contains no business rules of its own, no persistence or transport code and no framework logic.

GetOrderUseCase is a thin application-layer use case. Its only job is orchestration: it receives a domain repository port through the constructor, hands loading off to an application helper (loadOrder), and maps the result to a DTO (toOrderDto). The file has no persistence, transport or framework logic, and it doesn't contain any domain business rules. Coordinating a use case and mapping to DTOs are both normal application-layer jobs.

The file only maps the domain Order aggregate to an application-level OrderDto. Turning domain objects into use-case output DTOs is an application-layer job. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework logic, and it contains no business rules or invariants. Its only formatting is turning Date values into ISO strings for the DTO, which is ordinary DTO shaping. The graph shows that only application use cases consume it, which fits its role.

src/application/OrderLoader.ts is a small application-layer helper. It loads an aggregate through a domain repository port and throws a domain NotFoundError when the aggregate is missing. Fetching an aggregate through a port and handling the not-found case is ordinary application-layer orchestration that the use cases share. The file has no persistence code (no SQL and no database client), no transport or framework logic (no HTTP and no request or response handling), and no business rules beyond checking whether the order exists. Its responsibilities match the application layer.

PlaceOrderUseCase.ts is a standard application-layer use case. It turns input into domain value objects (Quantity.of) and hands order creation to the domain factory Order.place. It then coordinates the domain services and ports it receives through the constructor (StockReservationService, OrderRepository, IdGenerator, Clock) and maps the result to a DTO. The file has no persistence code (it calls the save port but does not implement it), no transport or framework logic, and no business rules of its own. Invariants and business decisions stay in the domain. All of this matches the role of the application layer.

src/application/dtos.ts contains only readonly interface declarations for use-case input and output data: OrderLineInput, PlaceOrderInput, OrderLineDto, OrderDto and StockLevelDto. These data transfer objects form the application layer's boundary contract. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic. It reuses the domain OrderStatus type and represents timestamps as strings, which suits DTOs. Every responsibility fits the application layer.

src/domain/Clock.ts only declares the abstract port interface `Clock` with a single `now(): Date` method. It has no implementation. That means no system-time access, no persistence, no transport and no framework logic. Defining a time abstraction as a port in the domain layer fits the domain role. The concrete implementation (SystemClock) lives in infrastructure and implements this interface, and the application use cases inject it through their constructors. That is the expected split between port and adapter.

src/domain/IdGenerator.ts only declares the IdGenerator interface, which has a single method, next(): string. It has no persistence, transport, framework or implementation logic. This is a domain port: the domain owns the abstraction, the application layer receives it through constructor injection (PlaceOrderUseCase), and the infrastructure layer implements it (UuidIdGenerator). Declaring a port in the domain layer fits the domain's role. No ADR prose was given.

src/domain/OrderLine.ts declares one immutable interface, OrderLine, made of a productId and a Quantity value object. That is a plain domain model shape with no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic, so its only responsibility fits the domain layer's role.

src/domain/OrderRepository.ts holds only a repository port, the OrderRepository interface. Its methods are findById, findByStatus, findAll and save, and they are written in terms of the domain types Order and OrderStatus. The file has no persistence implementation, transport logic, framework code or orchestration. Declaring a repository abstraction in the domain layer is a normal domain responsibility. The concrete version, InMemoryOrderRepository, is in the infrastructure layer, and application use cases get the interface through their constructors. The comment explaining why the methods are synchronous refers to atomicity, which is a design constraint on the contract and not infrastructure logic.

src/domain/OrderStatus.ts holds only domain concepts: the set of order statuses, the order in which an order moves through fulfilment, which statuses can still be cancelled, and a type guard for status values. None of it is persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic. isOrderStatus is a type check on the domain's own vocabulary, not request parsing tied to any transport. Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

src/domain/Product.ts is a pure domain entity. It holds stock state (onHand and reserved) and enforces business invariants: validation when the product is created, checking availability before a reservation, and the rules for release and dispatch. It raises domain errors. The ProductSnapshot type and the restore/toSnapshot methods are a plain-data memento. They use no persistence technology, ORM, SQL, serialization format or I/O, so the entity can be rebuilt without depending on infrastructure. Nothing in the file is transport, framework or application orchestration logic. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/errors.ts only defines domain error types: an abstract DomainError base class and subclasses for validation failures, missing entities, insufficient stock and invalid order state transitions. These describe business-rule violations in domain terms. The file contains no persistence, transport, HTTP status mapping, framework logic or application orchestration. The messages and fields (productId, requested, available, from/to states) use domain language. Its responsibilities fit the domain layer.

InMemoryOrderRepository is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the domain port OrderRepository and only handles storage: it keeps OrderSnapshot rows in a Map, rebuilds entities with Order.restore, and turns them back into snapshots with order.toSnapshot. findByStatus filters rows by a status value the caller passes in. That is a query, not a business rule. The file has no domain decisions, invariants, state transitions or use-case orchestration. Every responsibility it carries is persistence, which belongs in the infrastructure layer.

OrderController is an Express HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer, and HTTP transport is an infrastructure job. Its methods only wire routes, delegate request parsing to infrastructure helpers, call application use cases and turn the results into HTTP responses (status codes, the Location header, JSON). The ACTIONS table maps URL path segments to target OrderStatus values. That is routing, not business logic: it adds no checks on transitions, guards or invariants. Those decisions are left to AdvanceOrderUseCase and the domain. The file does no persistence work and sets no domain rules, so everything in it fits the infrastructure (inbound adapter) role.

The file src/infrastructure/UuidIdGenerator.ts is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the domain port IdGenerator using node:crypto's randomUUID. Wrapping a platform or library API behind a domain-defined interface is exactly what the infrastructure layer is for. The file contains no business rules, no domain invariants, no application orchestration and no presentation logic, so every responsibility in it fits its declared layer.

The file holds startup data and a seeding routine that runs at bootstrap. It builds domain Product entities with the domain factory (Product.create) and saves them through the ProductRepository port. It is called from src/infrastructure/app.ts, the composition root. Loading fixture data at startup is a bootstrap concern, which belongs in infrastructure. The file has no business rules of its own, such as validation, invariants or pricing logic. Those stay in the domain factory. It also has no transport or presentation logic, and it does not orchestrate any use case that would belong in the application layer. Its responsibilities match the infrastructure layer.

The file is an Express transport adapter. It maps domain error types to HTTP status codes, turns body-parser client errors into 4xx responses, handles unmatched routes and logs unexpected errors before returning a 500. All of this is transport and framework work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer. The file contains no business rules. It never decides what makes something a validation error or a stock problem; it only translates error classes the domain already defined into HTTP responses. It does no persistence. Whether the file may import from the domain layer is out of scope for this rule.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the process entry point. It reads the PORT environment variable, starts the HTTP server with createApp().listen and logs a startup message. Reading config from the environment, binding a transport and wiring up the framework at startup are all infrastructure work. The file contains no business rules and no domain logic, so it matches its declared infrastructure layer.

All three files deal with one thing: the data shapes that cross the application boundary. OrderDto.ts and ProductStockDto.ts define output DTOs and the mappers that build them from domain objects. PlaceOrderCommand.ts defines the input command. Both mappers copy values the domain has already computed (line.lineTotal.cents, order.total.cents, product.available) instead of working them out again, so the totals and stock-availability rules stay in the domain. Every file follows the same conventions: readonly interfaces, money as integer cents, and `to*Dto` mapper functions. No rule or invariant is repeated across files, and none of them go around the module's own abstractions. productId/quantity show up in both PlaceOrderLineInput and OrderLineDto, but one is a request shape and the other a response shape, so this is not a duplicated invariant.

The module src/application/ports holds two small outbound port interfaces. Both abstract nondeterministic system services (time and ID generation) that the application layer depends on. They have the same shape and purpose: each is a single-method interface with no implementation. The same pattern is used for both: use cases inject them through their constructors, and infrastructure classes (SystemClock, CryptoIdGenerator) implement them. Neither file repeats a rule or invariant from the other, and nothing goes around the module's abstractions. The files form one cohesive concern: application-level ports for system dependencies.

The module src/application/services holds two small application-level helper services. Each wraps a domain repository so the order use cases can load aggregates and get a uniform not-found failure. OrderLookupService wraps OrderRepository. StockAllocationService wraps ProductRepository and also persists products after stock moves. Both deal with loading aggregates for use cases and handle a missing aggregate the same way, by throwing the domain NotFoundError. Neither file goes around the module's own abstractions: both depend only on domain repository interfaces and domain types. No rule or invariant is duplicated. The not-found check appears in both files, but it applies to different aggregates (Order and Product) and uses the shared NotFoundError, so the error rule lives in the domain and is not re-implemented here. The two files are separate classes, but they don't split into unrelated concerns. Together they form one cohesive layer of shared loading helpers used by the order use cases.

All ten files hold one application concern: order and product-stock use cases. Each is a class with a single execute method that returns DTOs built by the shared mappers toOrderDto and toProductStockDto. The use cases that fetch an existing order by id all go through OrderLookupService.getById (Cancel, Deliver, Get, Pack, Pay, Ship), so the not-found rule for orders lives in one place. The use cases that change stock follow the same steps through StockAllocationService.load/persist and StockReservationService (reserve, release or commit), and the stock rules stay in those services, not in the use cases. Order state changes are delegated to the domain methods order.pay, pack, ship, deliver and cancel, so no use case re-checks state transitions itself. Some calls skip the lookup service, but each one fits its job: ListOrdersUseCase calls OrderRepository.findByStatus/findAll because it is a collection query, and PlaceOrderUseCase creates a new order. GetProductStockUseCase does its own findById plus NotFoundError check. This is the only by-id product lookup in the unit, so nothing is duplicated within the module. PlaceOrderUseCase.mergeLines is a private helper used in one place, and nothing shown duplicates it. Import direction is out of scope.

Both unit files belong to the domain layer and serve one concern: domain business rules. DomainErrors.ts defines a single error hierarchy rooted in the abstract DomainError. StockReservationService.ts handles reservation across several products. It hands the per-product stock invariant to Product.canReserve, Product.reserve, Product.release and Product.commit instead of re-implementing it. When reservation fails it throws the module's own InsufficientStockError, not a generic Error. Neither file duplicates a rule, splits into unrelated concerns or bypasses the module's abstractions. The application-layer StockAllocationService may overlap with this service, but it is not a unit file and its source was not provided, so it was not judged.

The module is one coherent unit: the Order aggregate. Order.ts is the aggregate root. OrderLine.ts is its value-like line item. OrderStatus.ts holds the status type and its state machine. OrderRepository.ts is the persistence port for the aggregate. Each invariant lives in exactly one place. Status-transition rules exist only in OrderStatus.ts (FULFILMENT_SEQUENCE, CANCELLABLE_STATUSES, canTransition), and Order defers to them through its private transitionTo method instead of copying them. Line totals are calculated only in OrderLine.lineTotal, and Order.total adds those up with Money. The rules that an order needs a customer, at least one line, and each product only once appear only in Order.place. The repository port works only in terms of the module's own Order and OrderStatus types. Order.restore rebuilds an order from saved data without re-running the checks in place. That is a normal way to reload stored data, not a bypass of the module's abstractions. No unrelated concerns, duplicated rules or bypasses were found.

The module passes. It covers one concern: the Product aggregate and how it is stored. Product.ts holds the product, its stock rules and its snapshot form. ProductRepository.ts declares how stored products are found and saved, and it works only with the Product type. Each stock rule lives in one place. The 'available' getter is the only place that works out onHand minus reserved. canReserve uses it, and reserve calls canReserve instead of repeating the check. release and commit both use the private assertReserved helper rather than each writing its own check. Construction goes through the factories (the constructor is private): create checks the name and initial stock, and restore rebuilds a product from a snapshot. Prices go through the shared Money value object and quantities through Quantity, and neither file works around them. Nothing is split into unrelated concerns or duplicated. Import direction is out of scope.

The module src/domain/shared has two files, Money.ts and Quantity.ts, and both serve one concern: shared, immutable domain value objects. They follow the same pattern: a private constructor, a validating static factory (Money.ofCents, Quantity.of), an add method, and ValidationError from DomainErrors for invalid input. Each rule lives in exactly one place. Money's rule (cents must be a non-negative whole number) is enforced only in Money.ofCents. Quantity's rule (a positive whole number) is enforced only in Quantity.of. The two rules are different, so the checks are not duplicates. Internal shortcuts are sound. Money.add and Quantity.add call the private constructor directly, which is safe because adding two valid values always gives a valid value. Money.multiply goes back through Money.ofCents, so a fractional or negative factor is still rejected. No file splits into an unrelated concern or bypasses the module's own abstractions.

The unit has a single file, src/infrastructure/server.ts. It is a small composition-root entry point that does one job: start the HTTP server. It reads the port setting, builds the controllers through the module's own container (buildControllers), and creates the app through the module's own factory (createApp). It does not wire dependencies by hand or skip either of those abstractions. It holds no domain rule or invariant that could be duplicated elsewhere. The only thing it owns is the port default. The file serves one concern and uses the module's abstractions consistently.

Both files serve one concern: bootstrapping and wiring the application. container.ts's buildControllers() is the composition root. It creates repositories, the clock, the ID generator, services, use cases and controllers, and calls seedCatalogue once. seedCatalogue.ts loads startup data, which belongs with configuration. It depends on the ProductRepository abstraction, not the concrete in-memory class. It builds entities only through the domain factories Product.create and Money.ofCents, so product and price rules are neither duplicated nor bypassed. No invariant is duplicated across the files, and neither file goes around the module's abstractions.

This module passes. Both files deal with one concern: the HTTP transport adapter. createApp.ts builds the Express app. It registers the health check, the stock routes and the order routes, using the Controllers abstraction, then adds the not-found and error middleware. requestParsing.ts turns untrusted request input into application commands and domain values, and the order controller in the same module imports it. Neither file repeats a rule that belongs somewhere else. parseStateQuery calls the domain's isOrderStatus instead of keeping its own list of valid states. parsePlaceOrderBody checks only the shape of the body and says in its doc comment that business rules are left to the domain. Both files report errors with the shared ValidationError, and createApp goes through the controller and middleware abstractions rather than handling requests inline. The only exception is the small /health endpoint, which is fine for app setup.

Both files are thin Express controllers with the same job: turning HTTP requests into application use case calls and returning JSON. Neither holds domain rules or invariants. Request-body and query parsing goes through the shared requestParsing module (parsePlaceOrderBody, parseStateQuery) rather than being reimplemented inline. StockController doesn't need body or query parsing, so it doesn't bypass anything. There are two small style differences. OrderController injects an OrderUseCases bundle and uses a named IdParams type, while StockController injects its use cases one by one and writes the params type inline as `{ id: string }`. These are cosmetic. Neither duplicates a business rule nor goes around a module abstraction. The module is cohesive.

Both files deal with the same thing: Express terminal middleware that turns failures into HTTP error responses. errorHandler.ts maps thrown DomainError subclasses, malformed JSON and unexpected errors to status codes and a JSON error body. notFoundHandler.ts produces the 404 for requests that match no route. Both use the same abstraction, plain Express (req, res) handlers. Neither bypasses anything in the module, and both send the same { error: { code, message } } body. The domain-error-to-status mapping lives in one place, statusFor in errorHandler.ts. The body literal is written out in four places (three in errorHandler.ts, one in notFoundHandler.ts). That is a small repeated pattern, not a business rule or invariant copied in two places. A shared helper could factor it out, but this does not reach the rubric's fail bar.

Both files have the same job: in-memory, snapshot-based persistence that implements domain repository interfaces. The problem is the storage invariant written in each file's doc comment: "changes only become visible once a use case explicitly saves them." Each file enforces it with its own copy of the code, and the two copies have already drifted apart. InMemoryOrderRepository.save stores structuredClone(order.toSnapshot()), a deep copy, so later changes to the entity can't reach the stored record. InMemoryProductRepository.save stores product.toSnapshot() as-is. If ProductSnapshot holds nested objects or arrays shared with the live entity, changes leak into storage without a save, which breaks the guarantee the comment makes. Because the rule is duplicated instead of living in one shared place (for example a generic snapshot store or base class that does the cloning), the module has two different meanings of "snapshot". The duplicated findById/findAll restore logic shows the same missing shared piece. I can't see Product.toSnapshot, so I can't confirm a real leak, which keeps my confidence moderate. The divergence is still a case of the same invariant being duplicated and applied inconsistently.
violation_messages: save() stores product.toSnapshot() without the structuredClone that InMemoryOrderRepository uses. The module's shared snapshot-isolation rule ('changes only become visible once ... saved') is copied into each file and applied differently, so nested snapshot state may stay shared with the live Product. | Has its own copy of the snapshot-storage rule (doc comment, Map-of-snapshots, clone-on-save, restore-on-read) instead of sharing one module abstraction with InMemoryProductRepository. That duplication is why the two repositories have drifted apart.

rationale: The module has one concern: thin adapters that turn system-level nondeterminism (current time, random IDs) into application ports. Each file implements exactly one port and uses one platform primitive. No rule or invariant is repeated across the two files, and neither file goes around a port. Both files follow the same pattern: a small class that implements an application port interface.

This file belongs to the application layer. It declares output DTO interfaces and a pure mapper, toOrderDto, that turns the domain Order aggregate into a plain, serialisable shape that use cases return. Mapping domain objects to application DTOs is a standard application-layer job. The mapper adds no business rules: it reads values the domain already computed (line.lineTotal.cents, order.total.cents) and does not recalculate them. It has no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework code. Turning Date values into ISO strings is a neutral step that only prepares data for the boundary. It is not tied to any transport, so it fits here.

The file only declares plain, readonly input DTO interfaces (a command plus its line items) for the PlaceOrder use case. An application-layer command DTO is supposed to describe use-case input like this. The file contains no persistence, transport, framework, or business-rule logic. Infrastructure code (requestParsing.ts) depends on it, which fits it being an application-level input contract. Import direction is out of scope for this rule.

src/application/ports/Clock.ts only declares the port interface `Clock` with the method `now(): Date`. Defining abstract ports for the use cases to depend on is the application layer's job. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic. The concrete version, SystemClock, lives in infrastructure, and the application use cases inject this port through their constructors. Every responsibility in the file fits its declared application layer.

GetOrderUseCase is a thin application-layer use case. It gets an order through an injected application service (OrderLookupService) and maps the result to a DTO with toOrderDto. These are orchestration and output-mapping jobs, which belong in the application layer. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic. No ADR text was provided.

ListOrdersUseCase is a thin application-layer use case. It gets a domain repository port through constructor injection, picks between findByStatus and findAll based on an optional filter, and maps the results to application DTOs. All of this is orchestration, which is the application layer's job. The file has no persistence code (it only calls the repository abstraction), no transport or HTTP handling, no framework code, and no domain business rules. The status filter is a query parameter, not a business invariant.

This is a small application use case. It takes a domain repository abstraction (ProductRepository) through its constructor, gets all products, and maps them to application DTOs. That is plain use-case orchestration, which is the job of the application layer. The file has no persistence code, no transport or framework logic (HTTP, ORM, SQL) and no business rules of its own. All rules stay behind the domain abstractions.

ShipOrderUseCase.execute only does application-layer orchestration. It fetches the order through OrderLookupService and loads allocations. It hands the state changes to the domain: order.ship(clock.now()) and reservation.commit(allocations). It persists through abstractions (allocations.persist, the OrderRepository port's save) and maps the result with toOrderDto. The file has no business rules written into it, no concrete persistence or SQL, no transport or HTTP handling, and no framework code. Every responsibility fits an application use case.

src/domain/inventory/StockReservationService.ts is a plain domain service. It coordinates domain rules across several Product aggregates: it reserves stock for a whole order on an all-or-nothing basis, and it also releases and commits stock. It works only with domain types (Product, Quantity, InsufficientStockError). It has no persistence, transport, framework, logging, transaction or orchestration code. Keeping invariants across several aggregates is a normal domain-layer job. This review does not cover import direction.

Order.ts is a domain aggregate, and everything in it belongs to the domain layer. Order.place enforces business invariants: an order needs a customer, at least one line, and each product only once. transitionTo guards status changes with canTransition and records them in the history. The total getter adds up line totals using the Money value object. The intent methods (pay, pack, ship, deliver, cancel) express domain behaviour. restore and toSnapshot use the memento pattern with plain data. They do not use any persistence technology, ORM, transport or framework, and they do no serialization to a particular format. I found no I/O, no HTTP handling, no database access and no orchestration of use cases. The file contains nothing that belongs in the application or infrastructure layer.

OrderLine.ts is a pure domain entity/value object. It holds a productId, a Quantity and a Money unit price, and works out a line total through domain value-object arithmetic. It has no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/order/OrderRepository.ts only declares a repository port, the OrderRepository interface. Its methods (findById, findAll, findByStatus, save) are written in terms of the domain types Order and OrderStatus. The file has no persistence code, no transport or framework code, and no storage details. Declaring repository interfaces in the domain is a standard domain-layer responsibility. The graph shows the infrastructure layer providing the concrete class (InMemoryOrderRepository IMPLEMENTS the interface), and application use cases receive it through constructor injection. This matches the expected roles of the layers.

This file holds only domain work: it defines the set of order statuses, a type guard for that value type, and the business rules for status changes (the forward fulfilment path and the rule that cancellation is allowed only before shipping). It has no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration code. The isOrderStatus type guard validates a value against the domain's own status list, so it is a domain concern, not transport parsing. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/product/Product.ts is a domain entity. Its jobs fit the domain layer: it guards its own rules when it is created (a name is required and initial stock must be a non-negative integer). It holds the stock rules for reserve, release and commit, and works out available stock. It throws domain errors when a rule is broken. toSnapshot and restore are a memento pattern built only from primitives and domain value objects. They contain no storage, database, serialization-format or framework logic. They let infrastructure repositories save and reload the entity without the domain knowing how storage works. The file has no transport, storage, framework, I/O or application workflow logic.

Quantity is a pure domain value object. It enforces an invariant (the value must be a positive integer) and offers value-semantic arithmetic. It has no persistence, transport, framework or application-orchestration logic. All of its responsibilities fit the domain layer.

The file sits in the infrastructure layer and handles only HTTP transport and framework wiring. It creates an Express app, adds JSON body parsing, maps routes to controller handlers, exposes a trivial health check and registers the not-found and error middleware. These are all transport concerns that belong in infrastructure. The file contains no business rules: it does not validate order state transitions or calculate stock levels. The /pay, /pack, /ship, /deliver and /cancel routes only pass requests to controller methods. The health endpoint returns a fixed status and contains no domain logic. Nothing in the file belongs to the domain or application layers.

The file is Express middleware in the infrastructure layer. Its one job is HTTP transport: it sends a 404 JSON response for routes that don't match anything. That job belongs in infrastructure. The file contains no business rules, domain logic or application orchestration.

This file is an HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer. Its job is to turn untrusted request bodies and query values into application DTOs. It checks only the shape of the input: whether a value is an object, a string, a number or an array. It also maps bad input to a ValidationError. It writes no business rules of its own. Whether an order state is valid is decided by the domain's isOrderStatus, which this file only calls. Building PlaceOrderCommand from transport input is a normal adapter task. Nothing in the file handles persistence or orchestrates use cases, and it contains no domain invariants. Every responsibility fits the infrastructure (transport) layer.

The file is an infrastructure persistence adapter that implements the domain ProductRepository port. Each of its responsibilities is a persistence concern. It stores snapshots in a Map, rebuilds entities through Product.restore, and turns them back into snapshots through product.toSnapshot. It contains no business rules, validation, use-case orchestration or transport logic. Calling the domain's own restore and toSnapshot methods hands the domain logic back to the domain rather than duplicating it here. These responsibilities fit the infrastructure layer.

This file is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the application port IdGenerator by passing the call to Node's crypto.randomUUID. Wrapping a system or platform capability behind a port is exactly what the infrastructure layer is for. The file has no business rules, no application orchestration and no presentation logic, so every responsibility in it belongs to its declared layer.

SystemClock is an infrastructure adapter. It implements the application port Clock by wrapping the system time source (new Date()). Reading the system clock is an infrastructure concern. The file has no business rules, no orchestration and no presentation logic, so its only responsibility matches the infrastructure layer.

The application module serves one concern: the order and stock use cases. The not-found check is written once, in OrderLookupService.require, and all single-order use cases (Advance, Cancel, Get) call it rather than calling the repository's findById themselves. DTO mapping is written once in DtoMapper (toOrderDto, toProductStockDto) and every use case that returns a DTO uses it. Time and IDs come from the Clock and IdGenerator ports. dto.ts and errors.ts hold the shared data shapes and error types. Stock handling is split by use case into reserve, release and dispatch, which are different operations and not copies of one rule. State-change rules stay in the domain (order.advanceTo, order.cancel). ListOrdersUseCase reads the repository directly for list queries, which doesn't go around the lookup service, because that service only covers fetching one order that must exist. ValidationError is unused inside the module, probably because infrastructure's requestParsers uses it; this is not a split.

src/domain is one cohesive order-fulfilment and stock domain. It holds the aggregates (Order, Product), value objects (Quantity, OrderLine, OrderState), repository ports (OrderRepository, ProductRepository), one domain service (StockReservationService) and a shared error hierarchy (errors.ts). Each invariant has a single home: - Order state transitions live in OrderState.ts (FULFILMENT_SEQUENCE, CANCELLABLE_STATES), and Order.ts only calls nextFulfilmentState and isCancellable. - The rule that a quantity must be a positive integer lives in Quantity.of. - The stock-availability rule lives in Product.canReserve and Product.available. - The rule that you can only release or dispatch units that are reserved lives in Product.assertReserved. StockReservationService.reserve checks availability for every line before changing anything, so it is all-or-nothing. It calls product.canReserve and reads product.available rather than re-deriving onHand - reserved, so it uses the Product abstraction instead of bypassing it. The only repetition is that it builds the same InsufficientStockError that Product.reserve throws, which is minor. Product.create's check that stock on hand is a non-negative integer is a different invariant from Quantity's positive-integer rule, because zero stock is allowed, so it is not a duplicate. Quantity.add uses the private constructor directly, but adding two positive integers always gives a positive integer, so no invariant is skipped. One thing outside the rubric: the service's doc comment says every movement validates all lines first, but release and dispatch only validate each line inside Product as they go, so they can apply part of a batch before failing. That is a correctness gap, not a cohesion or duplication problem.

Both files deal with one thing: putting the application together and starting it. app.ts is the composition root. createApp() creates the repositories, services, use cases and controllers, then mounts the routes and error handlers on the Express app. server.ts is a thin entry point. It reads the port and calls createApp().listen. Neither file duplicates a business rule or invariant. app.ts builds every dependency through the module's own adapters (InMemoryOrderRepository, InMemoryProductRepository, SystemClock, UuidGenerator, OrderController, ProductController, errorHandler), and server.ts reuses createApp instead of building a second app. Nothing goes around the module's own abstractions.

The module has one concern: it is the HTTP layer over the application use cases. The work is split cleanly across the files: - The controllers (OrderController, ProductController) set up routes and pass calls to the use cases. - requestParsers.ts holds all the checks that turn request input into use-case commands. - errorHandler.ts is the only place that turns errors into HTTP status codes. OrderController reads request input only through parsePlaceOrderCommand and parseOptionalState; it never checks req.body inline. ProductController has no input to parse. The parsers check only the shape of the request: type checks and non-empty strings and arrays. Business rules such as whether a quantity is valid or whether an order can move to a new state stay with the domain. The parser also uses the domain's isOrderState instead of keeping its own copy of the list of states. ADVANCE_ACTIONS is only a table that maps URL path segments to target states. Which state changes are allowed is still decided by the AdvanceOrderUseCase and the domain. The error-to-status mapping appears only in statusFor. I found no rule or invariant written in more than one place, and no case where the module's own helpers are bypassed.

All three files deal with one concern: in-memory persistence of domain aggregates. The two repositories follow the same Map-backed pattern and each implements its domain port. The seed file fills the catalogue only through the ProductRepository abstraction and the Product.create factory. It never reaches into the private Map of InMemoryProductRepository, so it does not bypass the module's abstractions. No invariant is duplicated. The order-state filtering appears only in InMemoryOrderRepository.findByState, and product construction is left to Product.create. Seed data sitting next to the in-memory store is a minor placement choice, not a split into an unrelated concern.

Both files are thin system adapters that implement application ports by wrapping non-deterministic platform facilities: SystemClock wraps the current time and UuidGenerator wraps random ID generation. They share one concern, which is providing system-level sources of time and identity behind port interfaces. Each follows the same pattern (a class that implements a port and has a single method), so the module's abstraction is used consistently. No rule or invariant is duplicated across the files, and neither file bypasses the port abstractions.

AdvanceOrderUseCase.execute only orchestrates. It loads the order through OrderLookupService and hands the state-transition logic to the domain aggregate (order.advanceTo). It uses the Clock port for time, saves through the OrderRepository port and maps the result to a DTO. There is no persistence, transport or framework code, and no domain invariants are written out here. The one borderline line is the conditional `if (order.state === 'shipped') this.stock.dispatch(order.lines)`. I treat it as cross-aggregate coordination, which is a normal application-service job: it reacts to a state reached in the domain and calls a domain service. It does not compute or enforce business rules itself. A stricter reading could argue the dispatch-on-ship policy belongs in the domain, for example as a domain event or inside advanceTo. Overall the module holds together well. It is the order-and-stock domain model: entities (Order, OrderLine, Product), the order-status rules (order-status.ts), repository ports and a domain service. Error handling is uniform, since every file throws through DomainError. Order passes its status rules to order-status.ts (nextFulfilmentStatus, isCancellable) and does not repeat them. Line merging lives only in mergeLines. The problem is the insufficient-stock rule, which has two copies. Product.reserve owns it: if quantity > available, it throws DomainError("INSUFFICIENT_STOCK", "Insufficient stock for product ${id}: requested ..., available ..."). StockAllocationService.reserve repeats the same comparison, `line.quantity > product.availableQuantity`, and builds the same error code and message from Product's public getters. It does this so it can check every line before changing any product. That reason is fair, but the rule now sits in two places. If someone changes it in one place (for example, adds reserved limits or backorders, or rewords the message), the other copy drifts out of step. The service also goes around the entity: it re-derives the rule from availableQuantity instead of asking Product. The entity should expose a single check, such as canReserve(quantity) or assertCanReserve(quantity), and both callers should use it. This counts as a fail under the rubric's "duplicate a rule or invariant that should live in one place".
violation_messages: StockAllocationService.reserve has its own copy of the insufficient-stock rule (`line.quantity > product.availableQuantity`, with the same INSUFFICIENT_STOCK message) instead of asking Product. The rule is now split between this service and Product.reserve. Product should expose one check (e.g. canReserve/assertCanReserve) that both use. | Product owns the stock-availability rule in reserve(), but has no check that other code can call before reserving. As a result, StockAllocationService rebuilds the comparison and error message from availableQuantity.

src/domain/model.ts holds only domain responsibilities. It defines entity and value types (Task, User, Project, TaskStatus, TaskFilter), a domain invariant (markDone refuses to mark a task done twice), domain error types, and repository port interfaces. Those interfaces are abstractions with no persistence code, so they belong in the domain layer. The file has no transport, framework, persistence or orchestration logic.

src/infrastructure/app.ts is an Express HTTP adapter that is also the composition root. Its responsibilities are routing (app.post/app.get handlers), parsing requests (the body, param and queryString helpers), shaping responses (toDto serialises dueDate to ISO), mapping domain errors to HTTP status codes (the error middleware), and wiring the in-memory repositories into TaskManagementService. All of these are transport, framework or composition work, which belongs in infrastructure. The isTaskStatus and assigneeId checks in the POST tasks and GET tasks handlers are type checks on untrusted input at the boundary, and they use the predicate the domain layer owns. They are not business rules. Business actions (createUser, addTask, assignTask, completeTask, listTasks) are handed to the application service. No persistence logic or business invariants are coded here.

The file contains only in-memory persistence adapters. They implement repository interfaces declared in the domain layer. Each class stores entities in a Map and retrieves them by id. InMemoryTaskRepository.findByProject only applies the query criteria given by TaskFilter (projectId, status, assigneeId), which is ordinary repository querying and not a business rule. Nothing in the file is domain policy, application orchestration or presentation logic, so every responsibility fits the infrastructure layer.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is a startup entry point. It reads the port from the environment, builds the app with createApp() and starts an HTTP listener. All of that is runtime and transport work, which belongs in an infrastructure-layer file. The file has no business rules, domain logic or application orchestration.

The src/application module is one cohesive application-service layer. dtos.ts defines the inputs and outputs for the use cases. InventoryService (addProduct, listProducts) and OrderService (placeOrder, advanceOrder, cancelOrder, listOrders) coordinate domain objects through the ProductRepository and OrderRepository interfaces they receive in their constructors. Both services use the same pattern: repository access, then a domain operation, then a private toDto mapping. Stock rules are handled by domain methods (canReserve, reserve, release), and order state changes by Order methods (advanceTo, cancel); the services do not reimplement them. Rules that live in the services appear only once within the unit: item validation and merging in normaliseLines, not-found handling in requireOrder and requireProduct, and the duplicate-product check in addProduct. The one repetition is the inline item type { productId, quantity } in CreateOrderInput and OrderDto. That is repeated type structure, not a duplicated rule. Whether the customer and quantity checks are repeated in the domain can't be confirmed from the material given.

All four files deal with one concern: the order and inventory domain model. errors.ts defines the error hierarchy. order.ts and product.ts are the entities and enforce their own rules. repositories.ts declares the persistence ports for those entities. Both entities raise errors through the module's own DomainError hierarchy. Neither creates plain Error objects or goes around the shared types. Each rule has a single home. Order state transitions live in the NEXT_STATE table, which advanceTo uses, alongside the rules inside cancel. Quantity validation lives in the private assertPositiveQuantity method. Stock sufficiency lives in canReserve, which reserve reuses. Two small things are not violations. First, reserve checks the quantity twice: once directly and again through canReserve. Both calls go to the same private method, so the rule is not copied. Second, Order does not validate the quantity on each OrderLine. That is a gap in what Order checks, not a duplicated or split rule.

The four files make up one coherent infrastructure adapter module for the order-fulfilment API. Two files are in-memory persistence adapters that implement domain repository ports. One file is the Express HTTP adapter. The last is the composition root that wires them together. Both repositories follow the same pattern: a private Map with findById, save and a list method. They use the domain abstractions (OrderRepository, ProductRepository, Order, Product) consistently. OrderController works only through the application services InventoryService and OrderService. It does not reach into the repositories, so it doesn't bypass the module's abstractions. server.ts only builds and wires objects and holds no business rules. One minor concern: OrderController hard-codes ORDER_STATES, a runtime list that mirrors the OrderState union from src/domain/order.ts. If the domain adds a state, this list could fall out of sync. It is typed as readonly OrderState[], so it can never hold an invalid value, and it exists only to validate the query string at the HTTP boundary. No rule is duplicated between files inside the unit. I don't think this one boundary-validation list is enough to fail the module, which is why my confidence is moderate.

src/application/dtos.ts only declares the input and output data shapes for application use cases: CreateProductInput, CreateOrderInput, ProductDto and OrderDto. Defining use-case DTOs is part of the application layer's role. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic, and it holds only type declarations. It reuses the domain OrderState type, which is an import-direction matter and out of scope here.

InventoryService is a standard application service. It coordinates use cases: it checks for an existing product through the repository port, builds the Product entity, saves it, and maps the result to a DTO. It contains no persistence code (no SQL, file I/O or ORM), no transport or framework logic (no HTTP, request or response handling), and no presentation concerns. The duplicate-ID check needs a repository lookup, so it is ordinary use-case coordination that fits the application layer, not an entity-level business rule. Mapping to DTOs is also an application-layer job.

OrderService works as an application-layer use-case orchestrator. Each public method loads aggregates through repository interfaces defined in the domain, calls domain behaviour (Product.canReserve/reserve/release, Order.advanceTo/cancel and the Order constructor), saves the results and maps them to DTOs. The file contains no persistence code (no SQL, ORM or storage calls), no transport code (no HTTP, request or response handling) and no framework code. The check that stock is available across several products before reserving any of them is coordination between aggregates, which is a normal application concern, and the stock rule itself is left to the domain (canReserve). Some parts are borderline. normaliseLines checks for positive integer quantities and merges duplicate items, and placeOrder checks that a customer is present. These are input checks at the use-case boundary; they could arguably move into the Order constructor as invariants, but they are not clearly misplaced logic from another layer kind. The in-memory nextId counter is a weak identity-generation approach, not persistence or transport logic. No responsibility clearly belongs to the domain or infrastructure layer kinds.

src/domain/errors.ts only defines domain error types: a base DomainError and two subclasses (NotFoundError, InsufficientStockError). Each one names a domain-level failure and builds a message from domain identifiers. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP status mapping, framework logic or orchestration. All of its responsibilities fit the domain layer.

src/domain/order.ts holds only domain logic: the Order aggregate, its invariants, and its state-transition rules, which raise DomainError. It has no persistence, transport, framework, serialization or orchestration code. All of its responsibilities fit the domain layer kind.

src/domain/product.ts holds only domain-kind work. It defines a Product entity, checks its invariants when the object is constructed, and contains the business rules for reserving and releasing stock. The only thing it imports is domain errors. It does no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration work, so every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/repositories.ts only declares two repository port interfaces, ProductRepository and OrderRepository. They are written in terms of domain types (Product, Order, OrderState). The file has no implementation, persistence mechanics, transport or framework code. Putting repository abstractions in the domain layer is the usual ports-and-adapters setup. The graph excerpt agrees: the in-memory implementations live in infrastructure and implement these interfaces, and the application services receive them through constructor injection. Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

This file is an infrastructure-layer adapter. It implements the domain OrderRepository port with an in-memory Map, and everything in it is about storing and retrieving orders. findById and save are plain Map reads and writes. listByState filters orders by an optional state, which is a query criterion, not a business rule: it doesn't validate anything, change any state or make any domain decision. There is no transport, presentation or business-rule logic here. Every responsibility fits the infrastructure (persistence adapter) role.

The file holds one infrastructure adapter, InMemoryProductRepository. It implements the domain port ProductRepository by storing products in an in-memory Map. Its three methods (findById, save, list) only store and fetch data. None of them contains business rules, validation, pricing, invariants or orchestration. Persistence is the right job for an infrastructure layer, so every responsibility in the file fits its declared layer.

OrderController sits in the infrastructure layer and only handles HTTP transport concerns. It sets up Express routes, turns request bodies, params and query strings into application DTOs, sends each request to an application service, and maps thrown errors to HTTP status codes. It does not enforce any order lifecycle rules: which state changes are allowed and stock handling are left to OrderService and InventoryService. Two things are borderline. First, the local ORDER_STATES list repeats the domain's list of order states, but here it only checks that the query string holds a valid value. Second, input-shape errors are thrown as DomainError instead of a transport-specific error. That is a design smell, but the file still does not take on another layer's responsibility.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is a composition root and transport bootstrap. It creates the in-memory repositories, injects them into the application services, sets up the Express app with JSON body parsing, mounts the controller router, and starts the HTTP listener using the PORT environment variable. Wiring, framework configuration, and process start-up are all infrastructure work. The file contains no business rules, domain invariants, or use-case orchestration logic, so its responsibilities match the infrastructure layer kind.

The module is one file, src/application/order-service.ts, and it covers one concern: order and product fulfilment use cases. One class, OrderService, holds addProduct, placeOrder, changeState, cancelOrder, listOrders and listProducts, along with its own input/view types. All persistence goes through the injected OrderRepository and ProductRepository, and domain state changes go through entity methods (advanceTo, cancel, reserve, release). The module's abstractions are not bypassed. Not-found checks live in one place (requiredProduct, requiredOrder), and view mapping lives in one place (toProductView, toOrderView). One wrinkle: ensureStockIsAvailable takes a products parameter but discards it (`void products;`) and fetches each product again through requiredProduct. That is a redundant lookup and a misleading signature, not a broken boundary. Its stock check (product.stock < quantity) may repeat a rule inside Product.reserve, but that source is not provided. The pre-check also has a valid coordination job: it totals quantities per product across lines before any change, so an order fails as a whole. Overall the unit is cohesive.

The module serves one concern: the order and inventory domain. errors.ts defines the one error type (DomainError), and both entity files use it for every invariant failure. order.ts owns the order lifecycle: the NEXT_STATE table drives advanceTo, and cancel() holds the cancellation rule in one place. product.ts owns stock invariants, routing both reserve and release through a single private assertPositiveQuantity. repositories.ts declares persistence ports in terms of the module's own types (Order, OrderState, Product) and does not go around them. Nothing in the module skips its own abstractions or carries an unrelated concern. The only overlap is the positive-integer quantity check: one copy is inline in Order's constructor for line.quantity, the other is Product.assertPositiveQuantity. These guard different things (order-line validity versus stock reservation) and are small, so this reads as minor overlap rather than an invariant scattered across the module. A shared Quantity value object could be a later refinement, but this does not fail the rubric.

The three files form one infrastructure adapter for the order-fulfilment app: - in-memory-repositories.ts provides the persistence adapters. - order-controller.ts is the HTTP adapter. - server.ts is the composition root that wires them together. The repositories implement the domain interfaces OrderRepository and ProductRepository and contain only storage logic. The controller sends every operation through the OrderService abstraction and never touches the repositories directly. server.ts only builds the objects and connects them. None of the three files bypasses the module's own abstractions. One minor concern: order-controller.ts keeps its own runtime list of states (STATES) and its own list of state-transition route names. Both repeat the OrderState set defined in the domain. That repetition sits between this module and the domain, not between files of this module. It reads as input parsing at the HTTP boundary, which is typed against OrderState. Also, the domain file isn't shown, so I can't confirm that a canonical runtime list exists there to reuse. Inside the unit, no rule or invariant appears in more than one place, so this doesn't amount to a failure.

OrderService in src/application/order-service.ts does what an application layer should: it coordinates use cases. It maps entities to view objects. It contains no persistence, transport, HTTP or framework code. The only borderline case is ensureStockIsAvailable, which adds up the quantity requested per product across an order's lines and throws DomainError when stock is too low. The rubric's examples of failures are business rules in infrastructure or presentation files and infrastructure code in domain files, so this is not a clear violation.

src/domain/errors.ts declares only DomainError, an error type for violated business invariants. Domain errors belong in the domain layer. src/domain/order.ts is a plain domain entity and fits the domain layer. It contains: the OrderState type, the OrderLine value shape, a state-transition table (NEXT_STATE), and the Order aggregate. src/domain/product.ts holds only a pure domain entity. Product checks its own invariants: id and name must be present, and stock must be a non-negative integer. src/domain/repositories.ts only declares two repository port interfaces, ProductRepository and OrderRepository. Their method signatures use only domain types (Product, Order, OrderState). The file has no persistence implementation, transport, framework code or application orchestration. The graph shows the infrastructure layer implementing these interfaces (InMemory*Repository) and the application layer injecting them (OrderService), which fits their role as domain ports.

InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository implement the repository interfaces defined in the domain layer, and they store records in Map instances. The file belongs to the infrastructure layer, and everything it does is HTTP transport adapter work. It defines Express routes, pulls values out of the request body, query string and route parameters, and passes them to OrderService. It also turns the results into JSON responses and maps errors to HTTP status codes (DomainError gives 400, anything else gives 500). The private helpers stateFrom, requiredState and requiredText only check that the input is well-formed: a value is present, it is a string, and it is one of the known OrderState names. They do not decide what is allowed for an order, such as which state transitions are valid, cancellation rules or stock rules. All of that is left to the application service. The extra routes for /orders/:id/{paid,packed,shipped,delivered} are only routing shortcuts to the same changeState call. Two small smells are not misplaced responsibilities. First, the local STATES list repeats the names of the domain's states for input parsing. Second, the controller throws DomainError for input validation errors. Neither one puts a business rule, persistence or domain behaviour into this file.

src/infrastructure/server.ts handles composition and startup only. createApp() builds the Express app, wires OrderService to the in-memory repositories and the controller, and adds the JSON body parser. The require.main block reads PORT from the environment and starts the HTTP listener. Wiring dependencies, configuring the framework and starting the process all belong in the infrastructure layer. The file contains no business rules, no domain decisions and no application orchestration.

The three files form one coherent application layer for an ordering system. CatalogueService handles products and OrderService handles orders. Both get their repository interfaces through the constructor, convert entities with a private toDto, signal errors with DomainError, and share input/output types from OrderDtos.ts. Stock changes go through Product.reserve and Product.release, and order state changes go through Order.advanceTo and Order.cancel, so neither service bypasses domain or repository abstractions. Minor issues that don't fail the unit: (1) the same product-not-found lookup-and-throw appears twice inside OrderService, in placeOrder and cancelOrder; it's local to one file and could become a private helper like getOrder. (2) OrderDtos.ts also holds the product types ProductDto and CreateProductInput, so its name is narrower than its contents. (3) combineItems checks quantities, and Order may check the same thing, but Order's source wasn't provided, so this can't be confirmed.

The src/domain module covers one concern: the order-and-catalogue domain. Order.ts and Product.ts are the entities. OrderRepository.ts and ProductRepository.ts are interfaces for storing them, each working only with its own entity. OrderStatus.ts defines the set of status values, and DomainError.ts is the one error type.
