The module's abstractions are used consistently: every invariant failure throws DomainError, and status is always typed as OrderStatus, derived from orderStatuses. Order status changes and cancellation rules live only in Order (advanceTo, cancel). Stock rules live only in Product (reserve, release, assertValidQuantity). Two small overlaps exist. First, Order's constructor repeats the positive-integer quantity check that Product.assertValidQuantity also makes. Second, the nextByStatus map in Order.advanceTo lists the statuses in the same order as orderStatuses. The quantity check is a one-line check on two different inputs (an order line and a stock reservation). The status map is typed Record<OrderStatus, …>, so the compiler forces it to cover every status. Neither is a meaningful duplicated rule, a split into unrelated concerns, or a bypass of the module's abstractions.

This module is a cohesive infrastructure adapter layer. It holds the HTTP delivery adapter and composition root (HttpServer.ts), two in-memory persistence adapters that implement the domain repository interfaces, and a one-line entrypoint (server.ts). All four files serve one concern: concrete adapters and wiring for the application. The repositories follow the same pattern: a private Map store with findById, save, and a list or listByStatus method. HttpServer.ts uses the application services (CatalogueService, OrderService) instead of reaching into the repositories or domain entities directly, so it does not bypass the module's own abstractions. Status validation is not duplicated: it reuses the domain's `orderStatuses` through the `isOrderStatus` guard. There are two small issues, neither enough to fail. First, the 400 message in the POST /orders/:id/:action handler hardcodes the list of statuses ("paid, packed, shipped, delivered, or cancel"). Second, the handler blocks the action "placed" itself rather than leaving that to the domain. Both are input-validation details at the edge, not a business invariant that should only live in one place.

CatalogueService does use-case orchestration, which is the application layer's job. It takes input DTOs, uses the ProductRepository abstraction to check whether a product exists, builds the domain Product entity, saves it through the repository port and maps the result to output DTOs. It has no persistence code (no SQL, file, or storage details), no transport or framework code (no HTTP or request handling), and no detailed business rules. The domain entity's constructor still owns the product's rules, such as stock. The duplicate-ID check is usually an application-level concern because it needs a repository lookup. The private toDto mapping also fits the application layer. No ADR prose was given.

src/application/OrderDtos.ts contains only readonly TypeScript interfaces: the input and output data transfer objects (DTOs) for the use cases. Defining use-case input and output contracts is an application-layer job. The file has no persistence, transport, framework logic or business rules. It does reference the domain OrderStatus type, but that is import direction, which is out of scope here.

OrderService is an application service that coordinates use cases (place, advance, cancel, list orders). It works only through domain repository interfaces and calls domain behaviour (reserve, release, advanceTo, cancel) instead of reimplementing state rules. Undoing reservations in placeOrder is use-case coordination. combineItems does input validation and merges items for the same product, which is acceptable in the application layer. It's borderline because the quantity check could also live in Order, but it isn't a misplaced core rule. toDto maps orders to the layer's return shapes, and newId is a simple ID generator. The file contains no persistence, transport or framework logic.

src/domain/DomainError.ts declares a single class, DomainError, which extends Error, takes a message and sets its name. This is a plain domain error type with no persistence, transport, framework or HTTP logic. Its only responsibility is to represent domain-level failures, which fits the domain layer. The application, infrastructure and domain files that import it are only consumers, and dependency direction is out of scope.

src/domain/Order.ts is a pure domain entity. It enforces its invariants in the constructor: an id, a customer id, at least one line, and positive integer quantities. advanceTo holds the order status state machine, and cancel holds the cancellation rules. All of these are business rules, which belong in the domain layer. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, I/O or orchestration logic. Its only dependencies are other domain modules (DomainError, OrderStatus).

src/domain/OrderRepository.ts only declares a repository port, the OrderRepository interface. Its methods are findById, save and listByStatus, and they are written purely in terms of the domain types Order and OrderStatus. The file has no persistence code, transport, framework code or business logic. In DDD and hexagonal architecture, a repository interface is a normal part of the domain layer. The graph excerpt shows that InMemoryOrderRepository in infrastructure implements this interface, and that OrderService in application receives it through its constructor. That is the expected split. Every responsibility in this file fits the domain layer.

src/domain/OrderStatus.ts defines only a domain value set (the order lifecycle statuses) and the OrderStatus union type derived from it. These are pure domain concepts. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic. That fits the role of the domain layer.

src/domain/Product.ts holds only domain responsibilities. It is a domain entity that enforces its own invariants: id and name must be present, and stock must be a non-negative integer. It also carries stock reservation rules (reserve, release, and quantity validation) and reports problems with a domain-specific error type. It has no persistence, transport, framework, logging or orchestration logic. Its only import is DomainError from the same domain layer.

The file only declares a repository port interface written in domain terms (Product). In ports-and-adapters / DDD, repository interfaces belong in the domain layer. The file has no persistence, transport or framework logic. The concrete persistence lives in src/infrastructure/InMemoryProductRepository.ts, which implements this interface. Application services use the interface through constructor injection. The file has no responsibility that belongs to a different layer kind.

src/infrastructure/HttpServer.ts passes. Everything in it is infrastructure work: the HTTP adapter, request parsing and validation, mapping errors to HTTP status codes, wiring up concrete repositories and services, and starting the server. The business operations are left to the application services (CatalogueService.addProduct/listProducts, OrderService.placeOrder/listOrders/cancelOrder/advanceOrder). The isOrderStatus guard and the check that rejects 'placed' as a URL action only decide which inputs the transport accepts. They do not decide whether an order may move between statuses, which is left to OrderService/domain. sendError only translates DomainError and other errors into HTTP responses, which is transport work. One borderline point: the route handler lists the allowed actions itself, which is close to business knowledge. It is still input validation at the HTTP boundary, so it is not a misplaced responsibility.

This file passes. InMemoryOrderRepository is an infrastructure adapter that implements the domain OrderRepository port. All three of its methods (findById, save and listByStatus) only store and fetch data in a Map, which is the job of the persistence/infrastructure layer. listByStatus filters on an optional status. That is a plain query condition, not a business rule: it doesn't decide whether a status change is allowed, check any invariant, or run any workflow. The file contains no domain or application logic and no presentation concerns.

The file is a simple in-memory persistence adapter. It implements the domain-declared ProductRepository port using a Map. That makes it a persistence adapter, which belongs in the infrastructure layer. It has no business rules, validation, pricing or domain invariants, and no presentation or transport logic. Every responsibility fits the infrastructure layer.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is a bootstrap entry point. All it does is import startServer from ./HttpServer and call it. Starting an HTTP server is transport and framework work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, domain logic or application orchestration, so its only responsibility fits the role of its declared layer.

The src/application module is one cohesive application-service layer. CatalogueService handles product use cases and OrderService handles order use cases. Both depend on domain repository interfaces and return DTOs built only by the mappers in dtos.ts (toProductDto, toOrderDto), so the module's DTO abstraction is used consistently and never bypassed. Domain rules stay in the domain and are not repeated here: order transitions go through order.advance and order.cancel, and stock rules go through StockReservationService.reserve and release. The not-found check exists once, in OrderService.requireOrder. There are two small issues, neither enough to fail the rule. First, the inline line type `{ productId; quantity }` is written out twice in dtos.ts, once in PlaceOrderInput and once in OrderDto. Second, OrderService creates its own StockReservationService instead of receiving it through the constructor, which is a dependency-injection choice and not a cohesion or duplication problem.

The domain module covers one concern overall: products, orders, order status, repository ports and stock reservation. However, src/domain/stock-reservation-service.ts repeats the stock-sufficiency rule that Product.reserve already enforces, and it skips the module's own error types. Two places are affected: 1. **Insufficient stock:** the service checks `product.availableStock < quantity` and throws a plain `DomainError` built from the same message text that `InsufficientStockError` already produces. So the rule exists in two places, and callers get a different error type depending on which path catches the problem. 2. **Missing product:** a missing product is reported as a generic `DomainError` instead of the `NotFoundError` defined in errors.ts. Error-to-HTTP mapping in the infrastructure layer (src/infrastructure/error-middleware.ts is an incoming dependent) probably depends on these error types, so skipping them weakens the module's boundary. There is also a smaller issue: the order lifecycle is split. order-status.ts holds the forward transitions in `nextStatus`/`canTransition`, while the cancellation rules are hard-coded separately in `Order.cancel` in order.ts. This one is debatable and is not the main reason for the failure.
violation_messages: reserve() repeats Product.reserve's stock-sufficiency rule (availableStock < quantity) and throws a generic DomainError with a copied message instead of InsufficientStockError, so the rule lives in two places and the module's error abstraction is skipped. | reserve() and release() report a missing product as a generic DomainError instead of the module's NotFoundError, skipping the domain's own error abstraction.

rationale: The infrastructure module is one cohesive concern: the adapter and composition layer for a single order-fulfilment API. in-memory-repositories.ts holds the persistence adapters for the domain repository ports. order-controller.ts is the HTTP adapter, delegating to OrderService and CatalogueService. error-middleware.ts is the single place where domain errors become HTTP status codes. server.ts is the composition root that wires them together. The module uses its own abstractions consistently: server.ts builds the app only from its sibling exports, and the controller hands every failure to errorMiddleware through next(error) instead of setting error statuses itself. Each rule lives in one place: the valid statuses come from the domain's orderStatuses, and the error-to-HTTP mapping exists only in errorMiddleware. Minor findings that don't fail the rubric: (1) OrderController.router() repeats the same status check inline in two routes, but both use one isOrderStatus helper, so this is not a duplicated invariant; (2) the class is named OrderController but also serves the /products routes, a narrow naming issue, not split concerns; (3) asyncRoute only catches errors thrown synchronously, but all current handlers are synchronous.

CatalogueService is a standard application service. It runs use cases: in create() it builds a domain entity, saves it through a repository port declared in the domain, and maps the result to a DTO. In listStock() it reads all products through the port and maps them to DTOs. It has no persistence code, transport or HTTP handling, framework logic or business rules beyond use-case orchestration. Domain construction is handed to the Product entity. All of these responsibilities belong to the application layer.

src/application/dtos.ts only declares the application layer's input and output data shapes (CreateProductInput, PlaceOrderInput, OrderDto, ProductDto). It also has two pure mappers that turn domain entities into DTOs. Mapping domain objects to use-case DTOs is a normal application-layer job. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or HTTP code, and it holds no business rules. The mappers only copy fields. The one renaming, availableStock to stock, is a presentation shape change, not domain logic.

OrderService does the work of an application-layer use-case service. Each method loads an aggregate through a domain repository port, calls domain behaviour on it (Order constructor, order.advance, order.cancel, StockReservationService.reserve/release), saves it through the port, and maps the result to a DTO. The business rules sit in domain objects: status transitions in Order.advance and Order.cancel, and stock logic in StockReservationService. The file contains no persistence code (no SQL, ORM or storage calls), no transport code (no HTTP, request/response handling or status codes) and no framework wiring. Generating the ID with randomUUID and throwing NotFoundError when an order is missing are normal application-level jobs. The service builds StockReservationService itself instead of having it injected. That is a dependency-injection style choice, not a responsibility from another layer.

The file only defines domain error types: a base class, DomainError, and two subclasses, NotFoundError and InsufficientStockError. These classes describe business failure conditions, such as a missing entity or insufficient stock for a product. That is a normal domain responsibility. The file has no persistence, no transport details such as HTTP status codes or response shaping, and no framework logic. Turning these errors into transport responses is left to infrastructure files such as error-middleware.ts.

src/domain/order-status.ts holds only pure domain concepts. It defines the set of order statuses, the OrderStatus type and the state-transition rule (the nextStatus map and canTransition). These are business rules that belong in the domain layer. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, I/O or orchestration logic.

src/domain/order.ts holds only domain responsibilities. It defines the Order aggregate and the OrderLine value type. The constructor enforces invariants, advance() enforces status-transition rules, and cancel() enforces cancellation rules. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, serialization or orchestration logic. Its only imports are from domain modules (errors, order-status). This matches the role of the domain layer.

src/domain/product.ts is a pure domain entity. The Product class protects its own invariants: the id and name must not be empty, stock must be a non-negative integer, and quantities must be positive integers. It also holds the business rules for reserving and releasing stock, and it raises domain errors. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, presentation or orchestration logic. It only imports domain error types from the same layer. Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

src/domain/repositories.ts only declares the repository port interfaces ProductRepository and OrderRepository. Their method signatures use domain types (Product, Order, OrderStatus). The file has no persistence code, no storage technology, no transport and no framework logic. Defining repository abstractions in the domain layer is a standard domain responsibility. The concrete implementations live in infrastructure (InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository implement these interfaces). Application and domain services depend only on the abstractions.

This file is a domain service. It holds the business rules for reserving stock: it adds up the requested quantity per product, checks that each product exists and has enough stock before changing anything (so all lines succeed or none do), then calls product.reserve and product.release. It reaches persistence only through ProductRepository, an interface declared in the domain layer and injected through the constructor. Domain services commonly use repository abstractions this way. The file has no transport, framework, SQL or concrete storage code. The doc comment's mention of an "in-memory catalogue" describes the repository's behaviour, not code in this file. Every responsibility here fits the domain layer.

The file passes. It is an Express error-handling middleware, which is transport/framework adapter logic and belongs in the infrastructure layer. Its only job is to turn error types into HTTP status codes and JSON responses: NotFoundError becomes 404, DomainError becomes 400, and anything else becomes 500. That translation is a transport concern, not a business rule. The file holds no domain logic, makes no business decisions and does no persistence. It only checks which error type it received in order to pick an HTTP status. Import direction is out of scope for this rule.

The file holds in-memory persistence adapters that implement repository interfaces from the domain layer. Storing data in a Map, looking records up by id, saving, listing everything and filtering by status are all persistence work, which is what an infrastructure layer is for. The findByStatus filter is just a query (an equality match on status), not a business rule. The file has no transport, presentation or business-decision logic.

This file is an Express HTTP controller in the infrastructure layer, and everything it does belongs there. It maps routes to application service calls, sets HTTP status codes, serialises JSON and passes errors to Express's error handler. Its validation (isOrderStatus, singleValue, and the typeof checks on req.query.status and req.body.status) only parses and checks untrusted HTTP input before handing typed values to the application services. That is input handling at the transport boundary, not business logic. The actual business behaviour, such as placing, advancing and cancelling orders and listing stock, is delegated to OrderService and CatalogueService. The file contains no persistence logic and no domain decisions, such as status-transition rules or stock checks. Two minor points do not count as a layer violation: it throws DomainError for input validation errors, which is an odd choice of error type, and asyncRoute does not catch rejected promises from async handlers, which is a bug.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the composition root and transport bootstrap. It creates the in-memory repositories, wires the application services into the controller, sets up the Express middleware and starts the HTTP listener on a port read from the environment. All of these are infrastructure jobs: framework setup, transport and dependency wiring. The file contains no business rules, domain invariants or use-case orchestration. Import direction is out of scope.

The module's three files form one cohesive application-service unit for orders and the product catalogue. dtos.ts holds the boundary contracts, and both services use them consistently. Each service gets its domain dependencies by constructor injection and maps its own aggregate to its own DTO in a private toDto, so the mappings are type-specific and not duplicated. Neither service skips the shared repository abstractions or reaches into the other's concern. Two small points did not justify a fail. First, order-service.ts repeats the 'Product not found' lookup in both place() and cancel() instead of using a helper like requireOrder. That is local repetition inside one file, not a rule spread across files. Second, the pre-check `product.stock < quantity` in place() may overlap a check inside Product.reserve(). Its likely purpose is to validate every line before changing any product, so all-or-nothing reservation makes sense. I could not confirm a real duplicate because the domain source is not in scope.

The three files form one coherent domain module: - order.ts holds the Order aggregate and its state machine. - product.ts holds the Product aggregate with stock reservation. - repositories.ts holds the persistence ports, which use those same domain types. There is no split into unrelated concerns, and nothing bypasses the module's abstractions. The order state-transition rules live in one place (`nextStates`, `advanceTo` and `cancel`). However, two validation rules are copied rather than kept in one place: 1. The positive-integer quantity rule appears in the `OrderLine` constructor (order.ts) and in `Product.assertQuantity` (product.ts). Both use the same condition and the same error message. 2. The rule that a product id is required appears in the `OrderLine` constructor (order.ts) and in the `Product` constructor (product.ts). If either rule changes, both files must be updated together. A shared value object or guard in the domain module, such as `Quantity` or `ProductId`, would keep each rule in one place. The duplication is small, but it matches the rubric's fail condition of duplicating an invariant that should live in one place.
violation_messages: The OrderLine constructor repeats two rules that Product also enforces: quantity must be a positive integer, and a product id is required. Both use the same checks and error messages instead of one shared domain value object or guard. | Product.assertQuantity and the Product constructor's id check copy rules that the OrderLine constructor in order.ts also enforces. The quantity and product-id rules are each kept in two places.

rationale: The infrastructure module has one cohesive concern: adapters and wiring for the order fulfilment API. in-memory-repositories.ts holds the persistence adapters for the domain repository ports. order-controller.ts is the HTTP adapter and goes only through the injected application services. server.ts is the composition root that wires repositories, services and the controller. No file bypasses the module's abstractions: the controller never touches the repositories directly, and server.ts builds everything through the constructors. Inside the module, the error-to-HTTP mapping (handle), the id check (orderId) and the state check (isState) each live in one place. Two minor points don't reach a fail. First, the hand-written `states` list may repeat the domain's OrderState values; this couldn't be checked because src/domain/order.ts wasn't provided. Second, OrderController also serves the /products catalogue routes, which is a naming mismatch rather than a split concern, since it is still the single HTTP adapter.

CatalogueService is a use-case service, which is the job of the application layer. It coordinates the domain repository port (ProductRepository) and the domain entity (Product). It checks that a product id isn't already taken by calling findById on the repository. It saves through the repository's save method and maps entities to DTOs. None of this is persistence, transport or framework code: no SQL, HTTP or ORM details appear. Checking for an existing id through a repository is normal application-level coordination, not a domain rule that has been moved out of the domain. Mapping entities to DTOs also belongs in the application layer. Product construction and its own checks stay with the Product entity.

The file only declares the application layer's input and output data contracts (DTOs) as plain TypeScript interfaces. It has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic. Defining use-case input and output shapes fits the application layer's role. It reuses the domain type OrderState, which is ordinary. Import direction is out of scope for this rule.

src/application/order-service.ts does what an application-layer use-case service should do. It turns input DTOs into domain objects and loads and saves aggregates through domain repository interfaces. It hands state changes to domain methods (Order.advanceTo, Order.cancel, Product.reserve, Product.release), coordinates work across the Order and Product aggregates, and maps results back to DTOs. It has no persistence, transport or framework code. In place(), the check `product.stock < quantity` runs before any reservation is made. That looks like a pre-check so the multi-product operation either fully succeeds or makes no change, not a domain rule taken out of the domain layer: the rule itself still lives in Product.reserve. The duplicate-order check and the missing-entity errors are normal application-level coordination. The default ID generator (crypto.randomUUID) is an injectable collaborator, not infrastructure logic. The stock pre-check could be read as a borderline business rule, so confidence is moderate.

src/domain/order.ts holds only domain concerns. It defines the order state type, a state-transition table, an OrderLine value object that checks its own invariants, and an Order entity that enforces lifecycle rules: transitions go one step at a time, a cancelled order can't change state, and an order can't be cancelled once shipped. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP, framework, serialization or orchestration logic. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/product.ts holds only domain responsibilities. It is a pure entity with invariants (a non-empty id and name, and stock that is a non-negative integer) and the business rules for reserving and releasing stock. It has no persistence, transport, framework, I/O or orchestration logic. Everything in it fits the domain layer.

The file src/domain/repositories.ts only declares two repository port interfaces, OrderRepository and ProductRepository. They are written purely in terms of domain types (Order, OrderState, Product). The file has no persistence implementation, no transport or framework code, and no storage details. Defining repository abstractions in the domain layer is a standard ports pattern, and it fits the domain layer's role. The graph agrees: the infrastructure classes InMemoryOrderRepository and InMemoryProductRepository implement these interfaces, and the application services receive them through their constructors. So the persistence logic sits in infrastructure, not in the domain.

The file contains only persistence adapters. InMemoryOrderRepository and InMemoryProductRepository implement the domain-declared repository interfaces with Map-backed storage (findById, save, list, listByState). That is the job of an infrastructure layer. listByState filters by state the way a storage query would, and it does not encode any business rule. The file has no domain invariants, state transitions, pricing or validation logic, and no application orchestration.

The file is an Express HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer. It handles routing, request parsing, input-format validation and turning errors into HTTP status codes. All of that is transport work, which belongs in infrastructure. Every business action is passed to the application services: placing orders, listing them, moving them to a new state, cancelling them, and adding or listing products. The checks for a valid order state and a valid order id only make sure the request is well formed. They contain no domain rules such as which state transitions are allowed or whether stock is enough. One small concern: the `states` array repeats the list of OrderState values instead of getting it from the domain. That is a duplication risk, not a responsibility in the wrong layer.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the composition root and transport bootstrap. It creates in-memory repository adapters, wires them into application services, mounts the Express controller router, sets up JSON body parsing and starts the HTTP listener using the PORT environment variable. Framework setup, dependency wiring and process startup all belong to the infrastructure layer. The file contains no business rules, no domain invariants and no application orchestration logic, so it carries no responsibility that belongs to another layer kind.

The src/application module is the use-case layer for a small ordering system. CatalogueService covers product use cases and OrderService covers order use cases. dtos.ts holds the input and output shapes, and both services use them consistently. Both services work through the repository interfaces from src/domain/repositories.ts. Each one maps entities to DTOs in its own private toDto method, and neither bypasses the DTOs or reaches into infrastructure. There are some small inconsistencies, but none amounts to a failure: - OrderService repeats the "product not found" lookup in placeOrder and cancelOrder. It has a requireOrder helper for orders but no matching requireProduct helper. - advanceOrder spells out the target states as a string literal union instead of reusing the domain OrderState type. - placeOrder checks stock before calling Product.reserve. This probably repeats a check that reserve also makes, but the code comment says the reason: every item is checked before any stock changes. Product.reserve is not in this unit, so I can't confirm the overlap. None of these splits the module into unrelated concerns or bypasses its abstractions. None of them clearly duplicates a rule that lives elsewhere inside the unit.

The four files cover one concern: the order and catalogue domain. - **`errors.ts`** defines a single error hierarchy rooted at `DomainError`. - **`order.ts`** and **`product.ts`** each hold one entity. Each keeps its own rules inside the class: the order state machine (`nextState`, `advanceTo`, `cancel`) and the stock rules (`reserve`, `release`). Both throw the module's own error types and never a bare `Error`. - **`repositories.ts`** defines repository interfaces for the module's own `Product`, `Order` and `OrderState` types. No file bypasses a shared abstraction. The `OrderState` type comes from `orderStates` in one place, and the transition rules exist only in `Order`. One small repeated check: "quantity must be a positive integer" appears in both the `Order` constructor and `Product.assertQuantity`. These guard different things, though. One checks that an order item is well formed; the other checks a stock-reservation argument. Each check sits in its owning entity, and no shared invariant has drifted between them. This is too minor to count as a split or a bypass. A shared `Quantity` value object would be a reasonable future cleanup, but the rubric doesn't require it. `NotFoundError` is declared here but only used by the application layer. Since it belongs to the domain's error vocabulary, this is consistent.

The infrastructure module has one cohesive concern: the adapters for the domain and application layers plus the code that wires them together. in-memory-repositories.ts implements the domain repository interfaces as pure storage. order-controller.ts maps HTTP requests to the application services, with error handling in one place, handle(). server.ts creates the repositories, services and controller. The controller goes only through the application services, never the repositories. Order-state validation uses the domain's orderStates list instead of its own copy, and the rules for allowed transitions stay behind OrderService.advanceOrder. Minor points that are not violations: the transition() parameter type lists the target state names by hand instead of taking them from OrderState. OrderController also serves the /products routes, so its name is narrower than its role. idFrom reports a missing id as a DomainError, which comes back as 409.

CatalogueService does what an application service should. It coordinates use cases (addProduct, listProducts) through the domain's ProductRepository port. It hands entity construction to the domain Product class and maps entities to application DTOs. The duplicate-id check in addProduct needs a repository lookup, which no single aggregate can do on its own, so it is normal for an application service to handle it. The file has no persistence code, no transport or HTTP handling, and no framework code. It also has no business rules that should sit inside the Product entity.

The file src/application/dtos.ts only declares data transfer object interfaces (CreateProductDto, PlaceOrderDto, ProductDto, OrderDto). These are the input and output contracts of application use cases, which is a normal job for the application layer. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or business-rule logic. It has no functions or statements beyond type declarations and one type import of OrderState. All of its responsibilities fit the application layer kind.

OrderService behaves like a normal application-layer use-case service. It loads aggregates through domain repository interfaces, coordinates operations across aggregates (it reserves product stock and creates an Order, and it cancels an order and releases its stock), saves through those repository ports, and maps entities to DTOs. The file has no persistence code (no SQL, storage or ORM), no transport code (no HTTP, request or response handling) and no framework code. Order state changes are handed to the domain through order.advanceTo and order.cancel. Stock changes are handed to the domain through product.reserve and product.release. Two parts are borderline but still fit the application role: - The stock check before any reservation (products[index].stock < items[index].quantity) is cross-aggregate coordination. It makes the order all-or-nothing, so no stock is changed unless every item can be reserved. This is not a core domain rule moved out of the domain. - combineItems validates the incoming DTO shape and merges duplicate product lines. That is input normalisation, which belongs in the application layer. Its "at least one item" check could also be enforced inside Order, but having it here does not move a responsibility to the wrong layer kind. The in-memory nextId counter is a weak ID-generation choice, but it is not infrastructure logic as the rubric means it.

src/domain/errors.ts defines only domain error types: a base DomainError and three subclasses named after business-rule failures (NotFoundError, InsufficientStockError, InvalidOrderTransitionError). The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP status mapping, serialization or framework code. The doc comment says these errors can safely be shown as client errors. That describes how callers may treat them, but the file doesn't do any of that presentation itself, so mapping to responses stays with the infrastructure controller. Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

src/domain/order.ts holds only domain logic. It defines the Order aggregate and its OrderItem value type, checks invariants in the constructor (id required, at least one item, positive integer quantities), and enforces the state-machine rules in advanceTo and cancel. Its only dependency is domain errors. The file has no persistence, no transport or HTTP handling, no framework code, no serialization and no orchestration of use cases. Everything in it fits the domain layer.

src/domain/product.ts holds a single domain entity, Product. It checks its own invariants: id and name must be non-empty, and stock must be a non-negative integer. It also carries the stock rules for reserving and releasing quantities, and it throws domain-specific errors. There is no persistence, transport, framework or presentation logic in the file, and no application orchestration. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/repositories.ts only declares the ProductRepository and OrderRepository interfaces. These are repository ports written in domain terms (Product, Order, OrderState). The file contains no persistence implementation, no transport or framework code, and no application orchestration. Declaring repository abstractions in the domain layer is the standard ports-and-adapters approach. The graph excerpt agrees: the concrete implementations (InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository) are in the infrastructure layer, and the application services receive the interfaces through constructor injection. Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

The file holds two in-memory implementations of domain repository ports, InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository. Their methods only store and fetch entities in a Map: findById, list, save and listByState. This is persistence work, which belongs in the infrastructure layer. The state filter in listByState is a simple query criterion. It makes no business decision such as a state-transition rule, validation or pricing. The file has no business rules, no transport or presentation logic, and no application orchestration.

src/infrastructure/order-controller.ts is an Express HTTP adapter. Every job it does is transport work, which belongs in an infrastructure layer. It sets up routes (routes()), reads and checks request parameters (idFrom, stateFrom), maps each route to a target state and passes it on (transition), and turns errors into HTTP status codes (handle). The real work is handed to application services: CatalogueService.addProduct/listProducts and OrderService.placeOrder/listOrders/getOrder/advanceOrder/cancelOrder. Whether a state transition is allowed is decided in OrderService.advanceOrder, not here. stateFrom checks the query string against the domain's own orderStates list. That is input parsing and does not copy any domain rule. Throwing DomainError for bad input is a minor oddity in naming, not a business rule in the wrong layer. No persistence or domain logic is embedded.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the composition root. It wires the dependencies together (in-memory repositories, application services, the controller), sets up the Express framework (JSON body parsing, routes), and starts the HTTP listener on a port read from the environment. Framework setup, transport startup and dependency wiring all belong in the infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, domain logic or use-case orchestration of its own. It only builds objects and passes them along.

The file has one clear purpose: fulfilment orchestration through OrderService and the FulfilmentStore port. It does not apply its domain abstractions the same way to orders and products, though. Order rules are handed to domain functions: createOrder, transitionOrder and cancelOrder. Product rules are written inline in the application service instead. addProduct checks for a non-empty id and name and a non-negative integer stock, then throws the domain's DomainError, so a domain rule is enforced in the application layer. The rule that stock must stay non-negative is also handled in three separate places in this file: the validation in addProduct, the `product.stock < item.quantity` check before the decrement in placeOrder, and the unchecked `product.stock += item.quantity` in cancelOrder. Stock changes are made by editing Product fields directly rather than through a domain operation. So the rule is split across several methods instead of living in one place, and the module skips the domain-function pattern it uses for orders. Confidence is moderate because src/domain/product.ts is not shown, so I can't confirm whether a product factory or stock operation already exists there and is being bypassed.
violation_messages: Product rules are implemented inline in OrderService instead of in one domain-level place. addProduct validates id, name and stock and throws DomainError. The non-negative stock rule is checked separately in addProduct and placeOrder, and stock is edited directly in placeOrder and cancelOrder. Orders, by contrast, are handled through domain functions (createOrder, transitionOrder, cancelOrder).

rationale: Both files belong to one domain concern (orders and products), but the module repeats rules and abstractions that should each live in one place. (1) The product-id invariant is implemented twice: once in createProduct in product.ts and again inside createOrder in order.ts, with the same message. The id rule is also inconsistent: createOrder checks the order id with `!id`, while the product id checks use `.trim()`. (2) product.ts declares two identical models, Product and CatalogueProduct, both with id, name and stock. That is two abstractions for one concept, and only Product is produced by the module's factory. (3) DomainError is the error type shared by the whole module, but it is declared in product.ts, so order.ts has to import it from the product file. This mixes a cross-cutting module abstraction into one entity's file. Because of the duplicated invariant and the duplicated model, the unit fails the rubric.
violation_messages: createOrder re-implements the product-id check (`!item.productId.trim()` → "Product id is required") that createProduct in product.ts already owns. This duplicates the invariant instead of keeping it in one place. Its own order-id check (`!id`) also handles whitespace differently from the other id checks. | CatalogueProduct has exactly the same structure as Product (id, name, stock), so the module has two abstractions for one concept. product.ts also holds DomainError, the module-wide error type, which puts a cross-cutting abstraction inside the product file.

rationale: The three files form one cohesive infrastructure boundary: http-app.ts is the HTTP adapter (createApp), in-memory-store.ts implements the application's FulfilmentStore port (InMemoryFulfilmentStore), and server.ts is the entry point that calls createApp(). The routes go only through OrderService and never touch the store directly. The store is used only via the port it implements. http-app.ts only checks the shape of incoming values (stringField, numberField, parseItems, parseState). parseState checks against the domain's own orderStates list rather than a copied one, so no domain rule is duplicated. Minor issues outside this rule: request-parsing errors are thrown as DomainError, so they return 409 instead of 400, and server.ts logs the raw parsed port even when it falls back to 3000. Neither splits the module's concern, duplicates a rule or bypasses the module's abstractions.

Most of `OrderService` is application work: it loads data through the `FulfilmentStore` port, calls domain functions (`createOrder`, `transitionOrder`, `cancelOrder`), saves results, maps not-found cases to errors and returns copies. Generating ids with `randomUUID` also fits here. Two responsibilities are domain rules written into the application layer: 1. `addProduct` checks the product's own invariants itself: id and name must be non-blank, and stock must be a safe, non-negative integer. It throws `DomainError` and builds the product as a plain object literal. That is entity validation, which belongs in `src/domain/product.ts`. 2. `placeOrder` and `cancelOrder` change product stock directly (`product.stock -= item.quantity`, `product.stock += item.quantity`). `placeOrder` also holds the rule that stock must cover the requested quantity (`InsufficientStockError`). These are rules about product state and should be domain behaviour, not edits from the service. Some of the stock check could be read as application coordination across several products. Even so, the invariant check in `addProduct` is clearly domain logic, and the application file signals this itself by throwing `DomainError`.
violation_messages: OrderService.addProduct checks Product invariants itself (non-blank id/name, non-negative safe integer stock) and throws DomainError. This entity validation belongs in the domain layer (src/domain/product.ts). | OrderService.placeOrder and cancelOrder handle stock rules themselves: the insufficient-stock check and direct `product.stock -=/+=` changes. These rules about Product state belong in the domain layer as Product behaviour, not in the application service.

rationale: src/domain/order.ts only holds domain concerns. It defines the Order and OrderItem types and the order lifecycle states. It also enforces the business rules: creating an order (validating ids and quantities, merging duplicate items), moving between lifecycle states in order, and the rules for cancelling. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP, framework or orchestration logic. Errors are plain DomainError objects, not transport-specific ones. Every responsibility fits the domain layer.

src/domain/product.ts contains only domain-layer work: it defines the Product entity shape, a factory (createProduct) that enforces business rules on id, name and stock, and a DomainError type. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP, framework or orchestration logic. CatalogueProduct has exactly the same structure as Product. That looks like duplication or a naming issue, not a responsibility that belongs to another layer kind. No ADR prose was provided to contradict this.

src/infrastructure/http-app.ts is an HTTP adapter. Its responsibilities are all infrastructure work: express route registration, transport-level parsing and validation of request bodies and query parameters (objectBody, stringField, numberField, parseItems, parseState), mapping errors to HTTP status codes in the error middleware, and default dependency wiring in createApp. Business operations (placing, transitioning and cancelling orders, adding products) are delegated to OrderService. parseState only checks input against the domain's exported orderStates list and does not define transition rules. One minor smell: transport validation reuses DomainError, so malformed bodies return 409 instead of 400. That is a wrong status code, not a responsibility belonging to another layer kind.

The file has one responsibility: it is an in-memory persistence adapter that implements the application-defined FulfilmentStore port. Every method is a simple storage operation on a Map: find, save or list. The one piece of logic is the optional state filter in listOrders, which is a query feature of the store. It is not a business rule or decision. The file contains no domain invariants, no application orchestration and no transport or HTTP handling, so all of it fits the infrastructure layer.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the process entry point. It reads the PORT environment variable, builds the HTTP app with createApp(), calls app.listen on the port and logs a startup message. Reading configuration, binding the transport and logging are all infrastructure or framework work, so they fit the declared infrastructure layer. The file has no business rules, no domain decisions and no application orchestration. Side note: the log message shows the parsed port value, not the fallback of 3000 when the fallback is used. That is a bug, not a layer-responsibility violation.

The unit is a single file, src/application/order-service.ts, and it mostly serves one concern: the order and inventory use cases behind OrderService, built on domain repositories, entities and DomainError. One part breaks the rubric. The file defines a private helper, requireProduct(id), to look up a product and throw DomainError("PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND", ...) if it is missing. cancelOrder uses this helper, but placeOrder repeats the same lookup and throw inline in its items.map callback, with the same error code and message. That puts the product-must-exist rule in two places in the same class and bypasses the module's own helper. A change to that rule, such as a new error message or code, would have to be made in both places. A smaller point: placeOrder also checks item.quantity > product.availableStock before calling product.reserve. Product.reserve probably enforces the same rule, but that file is not shown, so this is not cited as a violation; the comment shows the pre-check is deliberate. Putting addProduct and listProducts in OrderService is a mild mix of product-catalogue and order concerns, but they are closely related and not enough to fail the unit on their own. The verdict rests on the duplicated lookup and the bypass of requireProduct.
violation_messages: placeOrder repeats the product-must-exist rule (findById + DomainError "PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND" with the same message) inline instead of calling the class's own requireProduct helper, so the rule lives in two places and the helper is bypassed.

rationale: The src/domain module covers a single concern: the order and inventory domain model. errors.ts defines one shared error type, DomainError. order.ts and product.ts are aggregates that both signal rule violations through DomainError with codes. repositories.ts declares the persistence ports for those two aggregates and uses only types defined inside the module. Each invariant has a single home: Order owns state transitions and cancellation, and Product owns stock reservation and quantity validation. No rule is duplicated, no file goes around the module's own abstractions, and nothing unrelated is mixed in. One minor point: OrderLine.quantity is not validated in the Order constructor. That is a missing check, not a duplicated or split invariant, so it is not a violation of this rule.

The three files fit together as one infrastructure layer. `in-memory-repositories.ts` provides persistence adapters that implement the domain repository interfaces. `http-server.ts` is the Express adapter that calls `OrderService`. `server.ts` is the process entry point. Their concerns are related, and the repositories use the domain abstractions they implement. The problem is in `http-server.ts`. The GET `/orders` handler builds its own list of valid order states with `[...fulfilmentStates, "cancelled"]`, then casts the query value with `state as OrderState`. The full set of order states is a domain invariant. The domain already defines the `OrderState` type, but no runtime list of all states is visible here, only `fulfilmentStates`. So the HTTP adapter adds the "cancelled" literal itself and keeps a second definition. If the domain adds or renames a state, this check will silently drift out of step. That matches the rubric's fail condition: a rule that should live in one place is duplicated. A smaller concern: `createApp` is the HTTP adapter, but its default parameter also builds the in-memory repositories and the service. That mixes setting up dependencies with request routing, while `server.ts` is the actual entry point. This is a minor blurring of boundaries and not a failure by itself.
violation_messages: GET /orders builds its own set of valid order states (`[...fulfilmentStates, "cancelled"]`) and casts to `OrderState`. This duplicates a domain invariant in the HTTP adapter, so it can drift from the domain definition. The full list of order states should come from one domain-owned constant or validator.

rationale: OrderService is a use-case orchestrator, which fits the application layer. Each public method (addProduct, placeOrder, progressOrder, cancelOrder, listOrders, listProducts) loads aggregates through injected domain repository ports, calls domain behaviour (Product.reserve/release, Order.advanceTo/cancel), and saves the results. The file has no transport, HTTP, framework or concrete persistence code. randomUUID is an injectable default ID generator, not infrastructure logic. A few checks could arguably sit in the domain: the stock pre-check in placeOrder and the item validation and merging in normaliseItems ('at least one item', positive integer quantities). Still, the pre-check exists so that every line is checked before any reservation is made, which is multi-aggregate coordination and belongs in the application layer. normaliseItems is mostly validating and normalising use-case input. The state transitions themselves are left to the domain (advanceTo, cancel, reserve, release). None of these responsibilities clearly belongs to a different layer kind, so the file passes. Confidence is moderate because the order invariants in normaliseItems could reasonably be argued to belong in the Order aggregate.

src/domain/errors.ts only defines DomainError, a plain error type made from a code and a message. A domain error is a domain concern. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP status mapping, framework or orchestration logic. Other layers import it, but import direction is out of scope.

src/domain/order.ts holds only domain responsibilities. It defines the Order aggregate, its value types (OrderLine, FulfilmentState, OrderState) and its invariants: the constructor validates the order, advanceTo enforces the state machine, and cancel enforces the cancellation rules. Every error is raised as a DomainError. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, orchestration or I/O logic. Its only import is a local domain module, and import direction is out of scope anyway.

src/domain/product.ts holds one domain entity, Product. It keeps its own invariants: id and name must be present, and stock must be a non-negative integer. It also has the business rules for reserving and releasing stock. Its only dependency is a domain error type. It contains no persistence, transport, framework, serialization or orchestration logic. Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

src/domain/repositories.ts only declares repository port interfaces: ProductRepository and OrderRepository. Their method signatures use domain types only (Product, Order, OrderState). The file has no persistence code, no storage or framework details, no transport logic and no business rules that belong to another layer. Declaring repository abstractions in the domain layer is a normal domain-layer job (ports and adapters / DDD). The graph excerpt agrees with this: the concrete in-memory classes in the infrastructure layer implement these interfaces, and the application-layer OrderService receives them through its constructor.

The file passes: everything it does belongs in an infrastructure (transport) adapter. It sets up Express routes and parses JSON. It checks the shape of incoming requests and maps domain objects to response views. It also maps DomainError codes to HTTP status codes and wires in default dependencies. Every business operation (addProduct, placeOrder, listOrders, progressOrder, cancelOrder) is handed to OrderService, so stock and order-state rules are not reimplemented here. The query/body checks against fulfilmentStates only validate request input. They do not decide which state transitions are allowed. Throwing DomainError for bad input is a small stylistic coupling, not a business rule placed in the wrong layer.

The file only handles persistence, which is an infrastructure job. InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository implement the domain repository interfaces using in-memory Maps, with findById, save and list methods. The optional state filter in InMemoryOrderRepository.list is a plain query on stored records. It is a normal repository lookup, not a business rule. The file has no domain rules, application orchestration or presentation logic.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is a process entry point. It reads the port from an environment variable and starts the HTTP app that createApp() returns. Bootstrapping a server, reading env config and calling transport listen() are all infrastructure work. The file contains no business rules or application orchestration, so every responsibility matches its declared infrastructure layer.

The module has one file, src/application/fulfilment-service.ts, and it covers one concern: product and order fulfilment. FulfilmentService coordinates the injected ProductRepository and OrderRepository. Its view types (OrderView, ProductView, PlaceOrderItem) and private helpers (requireProduct, requireOrder, toProductView, toOrderView, combineItems) are used the same way in every public method. Each rule in the file lives in one place: not-found handling is only in requireX, view mapping is only in toXView, and input normalisation is only in combineItems. The file uses the domain's own types for its work: stock changes go through Product.reserve and Product.release, state changes go through Order.advanceTo and Order.cancel, and saves go through the repositories. One possible issue: placeOrder checks `product.availableStock < quantity` before calling reserve. Product.reserve may already enforce that rule. The code comment says the check is there so a failed request changes no stock, which is a coordination concern for the application layer. The domain source is not provided, so this duplication can't be confirmed, and a domain method such as canReserve would remove it. Similarly, the quantity check in combineItems may repeat a check in Order or OrderLine, which can't be seen either. With the evidence given, the unit passes the rubric.

The four files serve one concern, the order-fulfilment domain model. errors.ts defines the business-error type. order.ts and product.ts define the two entities and their invariants. repositories.ts defines the ports that persist those entities. The abstractions are used consistently. Both entities report every rule failure through DomainError. Order's state-transition rules live in one place: the orderStates tuple plus the advanceTo and cancel methods. Product's stock and quantity rules are also in one place: the constructor, reserve, release and assertQuantity. The repositories refer to the entity types and to OrderState directly instead of redefining them. There are two minor points, but neither is a rubric failure: - Order and Product each run a non-empty-id check. These are separate checks on separate entities, not one shared invariant that has been duplicated. - Order does not validate OrderLine.quantity. That is a gap, not a second copy of Product's quantity rule. No file bypasses the module's own abstractions.

The module is broadly cohesive as an infrastructure layer: http-server.ts is the HTTP adapter, in-memory-repositories.ts holds the InMemoryProductRepository and InMemoryOrderRepository classes that implement the domain repository interfaces, and server.ts wires them together at startup. However, http-server.ts repeats the order-state rule instead of keeping it in one place. The GET /orders and PATCH /orders/:id/state handlers each have their own copy of the orderStates.includes(state as OrderState) check. Both copies also throw an error message that hard-codes the list of states ('placed, paid, packed, shipped, delivered') rather than building it from the domain's orderStates, so the message will go out of date if the domain's states change. Input validation is also inconsistent: the file's own stringValue helper checks id, name and customerId, while productId and stock are checked inline. in-memory-repositories.ts and server.ts are fine.
violation_messages: The order-state check (`orderStates.includes(state as OrderState)` with the message 'state must be one of placed, paid, packed, shipped, delivered.') is written separately in the GET /orders and PATCH /orders/:id/state handlers, and the message hard-codes the list of states instead of building it from the domain's orderStates. This rule should live in one place.

rationale: FulfilmentService coordinates use cases. It loads aggregates through injected repository interfaces, calls domain behaviour (Product.reserve/release, Order.advanceTo/cancel), saves through the repositories and maps results to view DTOs. These are application-layer jobs. The file has no persistence code, transport/HTTP handling or framework logic. ID generation with randomUUID is a reasonable application concern. The pre-check of stock across several products in placeOrder keeps a multi-aggregate operation all-or-nothing, which is application orchestration. The request checks in combineItems (non-empty item list, product id required, positive-integer quantities, merging duplicate lines) could arguably sit in the Order aggregate. They read here as input validation for the command, which fits the application layer. Nothing clearly belongs to a different layer kind.

src/domain/errors.ts declares two error types. DomainError is the base for business-rule failures, and NotFoundError reports a missing domain resource by name and id. The file has no transport, persistence or framework logic: no HTTP status codes, response formatting or database access. The doc comment says these errors can be shown to an API client. That only describes the intent; it doesn't add any presentation behaviour. Converting these errors to HTTP responses presumably happens in src/infrastructure/http-server.ts, which imports this file. Defining business-failure error types is a normal job for the domain layer.

src/domain/order.ts holds only domain concerns. It defines the order lifecycle states, the OrderLine value shape and the Order entity. The entity checks its invariants in the constructor and enforces state transitions in advanceTo and the cancellation rules in cancel, raising DomainError when a rule is broken. Nothing in the file handles persistence, transport, framework code, I/O or the orchestration an application layer would do. Every responsibility fits the domain layer kind.

src/domain/product.ts holds a pure domain entity. Product checks its own invariants: id and name are required, and stock must be a non-negative integer. It also carries the stock business rules, reserve and release, and both reject quantities that are not positive integers. Its only import is the domain-local DomainError. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, logging or orchestration code. Every responsibility fits the domain layer kind.

src/domain/repositories.ts contains only two repository interfaces, ProductRepository and OrderRepository. Each one is written in domain types (Product, Order, OrderState). In a domain layer, these interfaces are ports: they describe what persistence must do without saying how it is done. The file has no storage implementation, I/O, transport code, framework code or business logic. The actual storage code lives in the infrastructure layer (InMemoryOrderRepository and InMemoryProductRepository implement these interfaces), and the application layer receives the interfaces through constructor injection. Everything in the file fits the domain layer's role.

The file is an Express HTTP adapter in the infrastructure layer. Its jobs are to register routes, check that request bodies and query parameters have the right shape, call the FulfilmentService application methods, and turn errors into HTTP status codes. All of these are transport and framework tasks that belong in infrastructure. The checks only confirm that inputs have the right type, and that the order state is a known value from the domain's orderStates list. That is input parsing, not a business rule. Business rules would be things like stock levels, allowed state transitions or cancellation rules, and all of those are left to the service and domain. One small point: the code uses DomainError for input-shape errors, and the error messages repeat the list of state names. Both are minor coupling, not business logic placed in the wrong layer.

This file contains only in-memory persistence adapters. They implement the repository interfaces declared in the domain layer, and storing and fetching records is the job of an infrastructure layer. Both classes keep data in a Map and expose findById, save and list. The state filter in InMemoryOrderRepository.list is a plain query parameter, like a WHERE clause, not a business rule. The file contains no business rules, no domain invariants, no state-transition logic and no application orchestration.

The file is the infrastructure layer's composition root and startup script. It builds the concrete in-memory repositories, injects them into the application service, creates the HTTP server, reads the port from the environment and starts listening. Wiring, configuration and transport startup are all infrastructure work. The file has no business rules, domain logic or application orchestration.

All six files belong to one concern: application use cases for project, user and task management. The problem is that the module's output boundary is not applied the same way everywhere. TaskDtos.ts sets up a DTO boundary (TaskDto, toTaskDto, CreateTaskInput), and the three task use cases return TaskDto. CreateProjectUseCase and CreateUserUseCase skip that boundary and hand the domain entities Project and User straight to their callers in infrastructure. So some use cases expose domain objects and others expose DTOs. The rule that a project must exist ("Project does not exist") is also written out twice, in CreateTaskUseCase and ListProjectTasksUseCase, instead of living in one place. The due-date validity check sits in CreateTaskUseCase rather than with the Task invariants. The DTO inconsistency is the main reason for the fail. The duplication is a smaller issue.
violation_messages: `execute` returns the domain entity `Project` instead of a DTO. This breaks the DTO output boundary that TaskDtos.ts sets up and the task use cases follow. | `execute` returns the domain entity `User` instead of a DTO. The module's output boundary is not applied consistently. | Repeats the project-existence rule ("Project does not exist") already written in CreateTaskUseCase. The rule should live in one shared place.

rationale: The src/domain module covers one concern, the task-management domain model. Its files are the entities (Project, User, Task), a shared error type (DomainError), a status type with a type guard (TaskStatus, isTaskStatus) and repository interfaces for the entities (Repositories.ts). The shared abstractions are used consistently: every entity throws DomainError when its constructor check fails, and Task uses the TaskStatus type both for its private state and for its status getter. Repositories.ts depends only on domain types. Each invariant lives in one place: each entity checks its own required fields, and Task.markDone is the only place that guards the move to done. Project and User have similar checks, but they protect different entities, so this is not duplication. One minor point: isTaskStatus lists the three status values again instead of deriving them from the TaskStatus type. Both lists are in TaskStatus.ts, so this does not split the rule across files. Nothing bypasses the module's own abstractions.

The src/infrastructure module is the app's infrastructure adapter, and its three files fit together. InMemoryRepositories.ts provides in-memory storage that implements the domain repository interfaces. TaskController.ts turns HTTP requests into calls on the application use cases, injected through the TaskApiUseCases interface. server.ts is the startup file that creates and connects everything. Each file uses the module's abstractions consistently. The controller works only through the injected use cases and never touches repositories directly, and server.ts uses the module's own repository and controller classes. Task status validation reuses the domain's isTaskStatus rather than redefining it, and every string check goes through one helper, requiredString. There are two minor smells. First, optionalQuery and optionalString do the same thing, so one is redundant, but both rely on requiredString, so the rule itself is not duplicated. Second, the error message in optionalStatus repeats the list of allowed statuses as plain text, and the method's name is misleading because it rejects a missing value. Neither is serious enough to fail the unit.

CreateProjectUseCase is a plain application-layer use case. Its execute method builds a domain Project, saves it through the injected ProjectRepository port and returns it. That is orchestration, which is what the application layer is for. The file has no transport, HTTP or framework handling, and no persistence details such as SQL, ORM or file I/O; it only calls the abstract repository interface. It also contains no business rules that should live in the domain. Generating the ID with crypto.randomUUID is a small technical detail that is reasonable for an application service to handle while setting up a use case. No other ADR prose was given.

This file passes. CreateTaskUseCase.execute does what an application use case should: it coordinates the work. It checks through injected domain repository interfaces that the project and assignee exist. It turns the input's due-date string into a Date and rejects invalid ones. It creates the Task entity, saves it through the repository abstraction and returns a DTO. Nothing in it handles persistence directly (all storage goes through repository interfaces), and it has no transport or framework code such as HTTP, request/response objects or server wiring. It defines no core business rules either; building the Task itself is left to the domain entity. Generating the ID with crypto.randomUUID is a small technical detail that is acceptable when a use case creates an entity.

The file passes. CreateUserUseCase.execute only coordinates a use case: it creates a User entity and saves it through the UserRepository port, which is injected through the constructor and defined in the domain layer. The file has no persistence code, no transport or HTTP handling, no framework code and no business rules. Generating the identifier with crypto.randomUUID could be seen as a technical detail. But it is a single call to a standard-library function that only supplies the new user's ID, not infrastructure logic, so it does not count as a misplaced responsibility. Which modules the file imports is checked by other tools and was not judged here.

The file is a typical application-layer use case. It runs a query through repository ports that are injected in the constructor, checks that the project exists, and maps the results to DTOs. It contains no persistence code, transport handling, framework logic or significant business rules that belong in the domain. The existence check is ordinary use-case input validation.

The file holds only application-layer orchestration. It loads the aggregate through the injected domain repository port, hands the state change to the domain (task.markDone()), saves the aggregate through the port and maps the result to an application DTO. It contains no persistence code, transport or HTTP handling, or framework logic. It also holds no business rules of its own, because the rule for marking a task done lives in the domain entity. The existence check that throws DomainError is a normal use-case guard.

The file holds the application layer's input and output DTO contracts (CreateTaskInput, TaskDto) and a mapper (toTaskDto) that turns a domain Task into a DTO. Defining use-case boundary data shapes and mapping domain entities to them is a normal application-layer job. The file has no persistence, HTTP or framework code, and it has no business rules or invariants that should live in the domain. Converting a Date to an ISO string is a plain serialization-friendly mapping for the DTO, not transport logic. The use cases depend on these DTOs, and so does the infrastructure controller, which fits a use-case boundary contract.

src/domain/DomainError.ts declares one class, DomainError, which extends Error and only sets the message and name. A domain-specific error type is a normal domain-layer responsibility. The file has no persistence, transport, framework or HTTP mapping logic, and it does not orchestrate application work. No ADR prose was given that conflicts with this.

src/domain/Project.ts declares a plain domain entity, Project, with an id and a name. Its only logic is a constructor check that enforces an entity rule (an id and a non-blank name are required) and throws a domain-specific DomainError. The file contains no persistence, transport, framework, or orchestration code. Every responsibility in it belongs to the domain layer.

The file only declares repository ports (UserRepository, ProjectRepository, TaskRepository) as pure TypeScript interfaces, typed with domain entities. It has no persistence implementation, no transport or framework code, and no storage details. Declaring repository interfaces in the domain is a normal domain-layer job under ports-and-adapters / DDD. The in-memory implementations are in the infrastructure layer (src/infrastructure/InMemoryRepositories.ts) and are wired in through IMPLEMENTS edges. The application use cases receive these ports through constructor injection. findByProject's optional status and assigneeId filters describe a query contract the domain needs, not a storage mechanism.

src/domain/Task.ts holds a pure domain entity. It checks its own invariants in the constructor (an id, project, title and description are required) and has one state-transition rule in markDone (a task that is already done can't be marked done again). It contains no persistence, transport, framework, DTO mapping or use-case orchestration. Its only imports are domain siblings (DomainError, TaskStatus). Every responsibility in the file fits the domain layer.

src/domain/TaskStatus.ts contains only two things: a domain value type (TaskStatus, a union of the allowed status values) and a pure type guard (isTaskStatus) that checks whether a value is one of those statuses. Both are domain concerns. They define and enforce what a valid task status is. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, or orchestration logic, so its responsibilities match the domain layer.

src/domain/User.ts declares a plain domain entity, User. It has two immutable identity and data fields. Its constructor enforces one invariant: the id must be present and the name must not be blank. When that check fails, it throws a domain-specific DomainError. All of this is domain work. The file has no persistence, transport, framework, or orchestration logic, so every responsibility matches the domain layer's role.

The file holds only in-memory persistence adapters, which is an infrastructure job: Map-backed save/findById and a filtered lookup that implement repository interfaces defined in the domain layer. The filter in InMemoryTaskRepository.findByProject is query/storage logic that a repository is expected to carry. It does not enforce business invariants, state transitions or authorization. The file has no domain rules, no application orchestration and no presentation concerns.

TaskController.ts is an Express HTTP adapter, which fits the infrastructure layer. Each of its responsibilities is a transport concern: - `router()` defines the routes. - `taskInput`, `object`, `requiredString`, `optionalString`, `optionalQuery` and `pathParam` check the shape of the request and turn raw body, query and path values into typed DTOs. - `handle` maps errors to HTTP status codes (DomainError gives 400, anything else gives 500). - Each route calls a use case through `execute(...)`. It holds no domain rules or state changes. For example, marking a task done, filtering tasks or creating entities all happen inside the application use cases. The status check calls the domain's `isTaskStatus` instead of redefining the allowed values. The required-field checks (title, description, name) only confirm the input is a non-empty string, which is ordinary request parsing, not a business rule. One small design issue: request-validation failures are reported with the domain's DomainError rather than a transport-specific error. That is a naming or coupling choice, not a responsibility belonging to another layer.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is the composition root and the HTTP server bootstrap. It creates the in-memory repositories, wires the use cases into the controller, sets up the Express app and its middleware, reads the PORT environment variable and starts the listener. All of these are infrastructure or framework jobs. The file has no business rules, domain invariants or use-case orchestration logic, so its responsibilities fit the infrastructure layer.

The module is one file, src/application/task-service.ts, holding one application service (TaskService) with use cases for projects, users and tasks. It also holds the input types and TaskDto those use cases need, plus two application errors (ResourceNotFoundError, InvalidInputError). It reaches data only through the injected domain repositories and the createId function. Validation goes through private helpers (requireText, parseDueDate, getProject), mapping goes through toDto, and the done state is changed only by the domain's task.markDone(). The status check `!taskStatuses.includes(...)` with the message 'Task status is invalid' is written out twice (createTask, listProjectTasks). Both copies use the domain's taskStatuses, so the rule is still defined in one place. It could be a helper like requireText, but this is minor and doesn't count as a duplicated invariant. I couldn't see whether the domain constructors also validate text fields, which lowers confidence.

The src/domain module covers one concern: the task-management domain model. That means the entities (Project, User, Task) and the repository ports for them. The Task status invariant lives only in task.ts: taskStatuses/TaskStatus define the allowed values, and Task.markDone with TaskAlreadyDoneError enforces the done transition. repositories.ts reuses that abstraction (TaskFilter.status is typed as TaskStatus) and does not redefine the status values. Each repository interface works with its own entity type. No rule is duplicated and no file goes around the module's own abstractions. Project and User are simple value-like entities, which is consistent with the module's approach.

The three files form one infrastructure adapter layer: persistence adapters, the HTTP adapter, and the code that wires them together. - **in-memory-repositories.ts:** implements the domain repository interfaces with Maps. - **task-controller.ts:** maps HTTP requests to TaskService calls and maps errors to HTTP statuses. - **server.ts:** builds the TaskService from the in-memory repositories and randomUUID, then registers the controller and errorHandler. Each rule lives in one place: - Request validation is defined once, in the controller's private helpers (body, requiredText, optionalText, routeParam), and every handler uses them. - The task filter semantics live only in InMemoryTaskRepository.findByProjectId. - Error-to-status mapping lives only in errorHandler. server.ts uses the module's own abstractions (TaskController.register, errorHandler and the repository classes) rather than going around them. One minor weak point: errorHandler recognises not-found errors by the string `error.name === "ResourceNotFoundError"`, while the other two error types are checked with instanceof.
