This bypasses an application-layer error type, not this module's own abstraction, so it is a fragility rather than a split or a duplicated rule within the unit. The `as CreateTaskInput["status"]` casts hand status validation to the service or domain instead of copying it, which fits keeping that rule in one place.

src/application/task-service.ts does work that belongs in an application layer. TaskService coordinates use cases: it creates projects, users and tasks, lists tasks and marks a task done. It works only through repository interfaces defined in the domain layer and an injected ID generator. Its other jobs are checking input at the boundary (required text, parsing the due date, checking the status value), raising application-level errors (ResourceNotFoundError, InvalidInputError) and mapping entities to DTOs (toDto). The file contains no persistence code: no SQL, no storage clients and no in-memory store. It also has no transport or framework logic, such as HTTP request or response handling, status codes or routing. Behaviour that changes state is left to the domain (task.markDone()). A few things sit near the line but are normal for an application service: the default status 'todo' and the check against taskStatuses are a use-case default and boundary validation, and checking that an assignee exists is cross-aggregate coordination. None of these is a domain invariant taken over from the entity.

src/domain/project.ts declares only a plain `Project` entity class with readonly `id` and `name` fields. It has no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic, so its single responsibility (modeling a domain entity) fits the domain layer kind. It is thin, but that is not a layer-role violation.

src/domain/repositories.ts contains only repository port interfaces (ProjectRepository, UserRepository, TaskRepository) and a query value type (TaskFilter). These are written purely in terms of domain types. There is no persistence implementation, transport, framework code or I/O in the file. Defining repository abstractions in the domain layer is the standard ports pattern, and the graph confirms that the infrastructure layer (InMemory*Repository) implements them and the application layer (TaskService) injects them. Every responsibility fits the domain layer's role.

src/domain/task.ts only does domain work. It defines the TaskStatus value set, the Task entity that keeps its state encapsulated, and the business rule in markDone() that a task can't be completed twice. That rule is enforced by the domain error TaskAlreadyDoneError. The file has no persistence, transport, HTTP, framework or orchestration logic. Every responsibility fits a domain-kind layer.

src/domain/user.ts declares only a plain User entity: a class with readonly id and name fields set through its constructor. It has no persistence, transport, framework or orchestration logic. A simple domain entity fits the domain layer's role. The import graph shows only incoming edges, from the application, domain and infrastructure layers, and import direction is out of scope for this rule anyway.

The file only implements persistence adapters for repository interfaces defined in the domain. That is the job of the infrastructure layer. Each class stores entities in a Map and fetches them by id or by query criteria. The filtering in InMemoryTaskRepository.findByProjectId turns the TaskFilter query parameters (projectId, status, assigneeId) into a lookup. That is persistence/query work, not a business rule. No domain invariants, state transitions or authorization decisions live here.

src/infrastructure/server.ts is a composition root and server bootstrap. It creates the Express app, connects the in-memory repositories and the randomUUID ID generator to TaskService, adds JSON body parsing, registers the controller and error handler, and starts the HTTP listener on a port read from the environment. All of this is framework, transport and wiring work, which is what the infrastructure layer is for. The file contains no business rules or domain logic.

src/infrastructure/task-controller.ts is an Express HTTP adapter, which is an infrastructure responsibility. It registers routes, reads the request body, query and route params, checks that inputs are well-formed (types and presence), passes the work to TaskService, and turns errors into HTTP status codes. None of this is business logic. Task status rules, assignment and completion are all left to the application and domain layers. The validation helpers only check request syntax and data types, which belongs at the transport boundary. errorHandler only turns error types into status codes (400, 409, 404, 500), which is presentation/transport mapping. The file does not access persistence directly and contains no domain decisions.

The module has one concern: application use cases for users, projects and tasks, plus shared DTOs and ApplicationError. The use cases use ApplicationError and the DTOs consistently. The problem is the mapping from Task to TaskOutput, which includes the rule that dueDate is serialized with toISOString() and that status comes from getStatus(). That mapping is written separately in three files: as a private toOutput in CreateTaskUseCase, again as a private toOutput in ListProjectTasksUseCase, and inline in MarkTaskDoneUseCase.execute. This logic belongs in one place, for example a shared mapper next to dtos.ts. The "name is required" check is also repeated in CreateProjectUseCase and CreateUserUseCase, but that is a smaller issue.
violation_messages: Has its own private toOutput mapping from Task to TaskOutput, which duplicates the one in ListProjectTasksUseCase and MarkTaskDoneUseCase instead of using a single shared mapper. | Has a private toOutput that is the same as the one in CreateTaskUseCase, so the TaskOutput mapping and dueDate serialization rule exist in two places. | Writes the Task to TaskOutput mapping inline in execute, a third copy of the mapping rule (dueDate?.toISOString(), getStatus()).

rationale: The src/domain module holds a single concern: the task-management domain model. It has three entities (Project, User, Task), a repository port for each (ProjectRepository, UserRepository, TaskRepository), an IdGenerator port, the task-status value set, and a domain error hierarchy. The abstractions are used consistently. Each repository interface follows the same save/findById shape, and TaskRepository adds a task-specific query (findByProjectId with TaskFilter). The status vocabulary is defined once in task-status.ts (TASK_STATUSES, TaskStatus, isTaskStatus). Task.ts and task-repository.ts both import that type instead of redefining status literals. The rule that a completed task cannot be completed again lives only in Task.markDone, and its error lives only in errors.ts (TaskAlreadyDoneError extends DomainError). No file duplicates an invariant, works around the module's own types, or brings in an unrelated concern.

The module covers one concern: infrastructure adapters for the task API. It has the Express controllers, the in-memory repositories, the UUID generator and the composition root (createHttpServer / server.ts). Grouping these together is reasonable for an infrastructure module. The repositories and UuidGenerator use the domain abstractions they implement correctly and consistently. The problem is one HTTP input-parsing rule: a missing or non-string field becomes "". The three controllers each re-implement this rule in their own way instead of sharing one helper: - ProjectController.create checks the field inline. - TaskController has a private text() method (plus more inline checks for dueDate and assigneeId). - UserController has a private stringField() method. The three versions also behave slightly differently. stringField guards against a null or non-object body. The inline `body?.name` cast does not do the same structural check. Inside TaskController, the task-status validation is also written twice, in create and in list: the isTaskStatus check and the 400 "invalid task status" error. The rubric treats a duplicated rule that should live in one place as a fail.
violation_messages: UserController.stringField re-implements the request-field string coercion rule. ProjectController and TaskController each have their own version of the same rule, with slightly different behaviour. It should live in one shared request-parsing helper. | ProjectController.create converts body.name to a string inline instead of using a shared helper. This duplicates the coercion in TaskController.text and UserController.stringField, without the null/object guard that stringField has. | TaskController.text is a third copy of the string-coercion rule. The isTaskStatus check with the 400 'invalid task status' error is also written twice, in create and in list, instead of in one place.

rationale: ApplicationError is declared in the application layer, yet its constructor takes a public readonly `statusCode: number` field. That field encodes how the error is sent over HTTP. HTTP status mapping is a transport concern, and here that concern belongs to the infrastructure layer (http-server.ts and task-controller.ts). The graph shows that five use cases import this class, so they must pick an HTTP status code when they raise an error. That pulls transport decisions into the application layer. An application error should describe the failure in application terms, such as an error kind or code like NotFound or Conflict. An application service should coordinate use cases. It should pass storage to repositories in infrastructure and leave entity rules to the domain. TaskManagementService does three jobs that belong to other layers: 1. Persistence (infrastructure): it stores users, projects and tasks in its own private Maps, creates IDs from counters, and looks records up directly. This is repository work with nothing between it and the use cases. 2. Entity rules (domain): checks such as "a task that is already done can't be marked done", the allowed status values, required title and description, and valid due dates are entity invariants. They are coded as private service methods instead of on the domain entities. 3. Transport details (infrastructure): it passes HTTP status codes (404, 409) when it throws errors, which ties the use cases to HTTP. The persistence job alone is enough to fail the rule.
violation_messages: TaskManagementService handles persistence itself: the private Maps `users`, `projects` and `tasks`, the ID counters `nextUserId`, `nextProjectId` and `nextTaskId`, and the Map lookups in getUser, getProject and getTask. This is repository work that belongs in the infrastructure layer. | Entity rules sit in the application service instead of the domain: markTaskDone's 'already done' check, requireStatus, validateDueDate, and requireText for title and description. | HTTP status codes (404 in getUser, getProject and getTask; 409 in markTaskDone) are passed to DomainError, which puts a transport concern in the application layer.

rationale: Most of src/domain/entities.ts fits the domain layer: the TaskStatus union, the User, Project and Task entity interfaces, and the taskStatuses list are pure domain concepts. The exception is DomainError. Its constructor takes `public readonly statusCode: number = 400`, which builds HTTP transport meaning (400 Bad Request) into the domain error type. Choosing HTTP status codes is presentation or transport work and belongs in the infrastructure layer. In this codebase that is likely the error handler in src/infrastructure/http-server.ts, which should map domain errors to status codes. The leak is small, but it is a transport concern in a domain file, so the unit fails.
violation_messages: DomainError carries `statusCode: number = 400`, an HTTP transport detail, so the domain error is tied to HTTP semantics. Mapping errors to HTTP status codes belongs in the infrastructure (transport) layer, for example in the http-server error handler. Domain errors should carry only domain meaning, such as an error kind or code.

The mapping itself is an ordinary infrastructure/presentation job.
